Workshop Summary: The team gets together at the start of a project to get to know each other as people, not just coworkers. Everyone shares things like their interests, how they like to work, what they are excited about, and what worries them. This helps the team feel safe with each other before the real work starts.
Workshop Goals:
Help teammates get to know each other as people
Start building trust and psychological safety
Learn how each person likes to work
Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Complete four activities with your team.
2. Follow the instructions in each activity section.
3. Run the intro activity: give time to fill out the template, then go around and share out loud.
4. Do the working style activity: place your name where you align on each scale.
5. Add hopes and fears to sticky notes, discuss briefly or invite people to review other’s sticky notes.
6. Run Crazy 6: draw six things about yourself. Invite people to explain their drawings and share anything they want to share.
7. Time-box each activity but leave space for natural banter and questions.
8. Have fun! It's okay if not everything gets done. The goal is team connection.
Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: People do better work when they feel comfortable with the people around them. Starting with a human connection makes it easier to speak up, ask for help, and share ideas later in the project.
How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Run this once at the start of a new team or project phase. You can also do a short version any time new people join the team.
Who Owns the Workshop?: The Agile Coaching function owns this workshop and is responsible for running it with the team.
Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have a shared understanding of each other teammate, their background, their interest, and their working styles.
Additional Details: When to use: at kickoff, in the first week, before the team digs into project work.
Workshop Pitch Statement: A casual first-day kickoff party where a new team gets to know each other as humans, laying the psychological safety and trust the next several weeks of work depend on.
What You Need Before You Start: This is the team's very first workshop, so no project prep is needed, just everyone present and willing to be a little playful. Set up the FigJam board with the four activity sections ready to copy, and bring a timer. An Agile Coach should be ready to facilitate and go first to set the tone.
The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. Who are my teammates as people?
2. How does each of us like to work, learn, decide, and get feedback?
3. What are our hopes and fears for this project?
4. What do we want to learn, and how can Tech Fleet support us?
What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave knowing each other as people, with a first layer of trust and openness in place. Done well, people laughed, shared a little of themselves, and feel safer speaking up. It is fine if not every activity finishes; connection is the goal.
Time Needed: About 45 to 60 minutes across the four activities
Common Pitfalls & Tips: Do not over-formalize it; the point is fun and connection, not productivity. Time-box each activity but leave room for natural banter. Facilitators should go first and share openly to make it safe for everyone else.
Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam; it becomes a living memento of the team's start.

# Agile vs. Waterfall Operations

  # Waterfall
    Agile vs. Waterfall
    There are two ways to build things through process:
Waterfall
Agile
Waterfall processes happen in sequential phases. Each phase must be complete before the next phase can begin.
Agile processes are flexible and handle work in parallel. There are no phases, there is only continuously delivering to users to gain feedback and determine next steps.
    The Waterfall Manifesto
    Waterfall Operations
    We’ve uncovered ancient ways of developing software and helping ourselves do it. Through this, we’ve come to value:
Processes and tools over interactions with individuals
Comprehensive documentation over working software
Contract negotiation over customer collaboration
Following a plan over responding to change

That is, we never value the things on the right. We’re rigidly following our principles. Forever.
    Waterfall is a process of building where:
Each team is “siloed”, working alone and handing off to the next when they are done
Everyone agrees to the scope of work in the beginning, and they never change the scope of work
Teams don’t collect feedback until they are finished with the project
No research work happens in the design phase; no design work happens in the requirements phase
There is no process built for adjusting previous work until the project is over
No one is validating their work with clients or users; they see it at the end of the delivery

    Agile Operations
    We’ve uncovered better ways of developing software and helping others do it Through this, we’ve come to value:
Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
Working software over comprehensive documentation
Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
Responding to change over following a plan

# Building Agile Teams that Perform
  The Basic Tenets of Agile Team Building
  Measuring the Agile Tenets
  Agile team strength is like a garden: you have to maintain agility and pick out the weeds to ensure health and growth of your team. How teams do this is open to the person owning the product, and the scrum master. 

Here are some key points to determine levels of self-organization, psychological safety, servant leadership, iterative value delivery, and continuous improvement.
  To measure Agility, teams must look at the components of what makes an Agile team agile: self-organization, psychological safety, servant leadership, iterative value, and continuous improvement. Here’s a set of checklists you can use to determine your team’s current state of agility.
  Self-organization: 

Allow the day-to-day people doing the work to make decisions themselves, instead of the people leading the team, and let the team carry out their own work in the way they want, or think is best
  Psychological Safety:

Build the sense of safety and belonging throughout the team:
Make every member of the team feel like they have room to speak their mind
Actively listen when others have things to say, and make team feel like their voice matters
Give the room for people to bring their own personalities and unique capabilities to the table in the way THEY want to do so
Allow room for team mates to challenge the status quo, and experiment with new ways of working
Encourage failing “fast”, i.e. failure and quick reflection and quick adjustment based on what the team thinks they should do
Let them take the risks that THEY decide to take, that could lead to failure or disaster, for the purposes of allowing them to build up decision making prowess
  Self-organization checklist
  Psychological Safety checklist
  Does your team wait for answers or initiate things on their own?
Does your team ask for clarity before starting or continuing work?
Does your team volunteer to work assignments?
Does your team contribute to conversations?
Does your team present new ideas for how to work, or idea for the product?
Does your team build consensus together and involve each other in decision making?
  Does your team speak up about concerns?
Does your team contribute to conversations freely?
Does your team voice dissent? 
Does your team celebrate each other for who they are and what they bring to the contributions?
Does your team experiment with new ways of working together? 
Does your team take risks together, and try new things?
  Servant Leadership:

All managers and all team mates should act as servant leaders to each other, those around them, those “above” them, or those “below” them in any organization’s hierarchy
  Servant Leadership checklist
  Iterative Value checklist
  Do your team members support each others’ growth instead of their own?
Does the person in charge tell everyone what to do, or do they transfer the power to the team?
Does your team show respect towards others? 
Does your team empathize with others and help each other?
Does your team seek to understand situations that arise, and communicate needs?
Does your team set expectations with each other in healthy ways?
  Does your team deliver work incrementally?
Does your team constantly involve clients,  stakeholders, and users in feedback sessions? 
Does your team collaborate with each other to determine the highest priorities to deliver in unison? 
Does your team work on the most important things at any given time, and deliver them quickly?
  Iterative value delivery: 

Teams should be empowered to deliver value early and often in order to gather feedback and decide themselves how they need to adjust. By doing so, and having self-organization, and psychological safety, the team can flag risks early or set better directions for them and for the organization.
  Continuous improvement:

Teams should be granted the opportunity to fail, and to build a process of quick adjustment when they fail. “Failure” is vague here: it could mean that the team’s plan didn’t work, or it could mean that something happened in the world requiring the team to change, or it could mean that someone made a mistake / didn’t do something.
  Continuous Improvement checklist
  Does your team have a “fail forward” attitude?
Does your team look at things in hindsight as opportunities?
Does your team look at problems as opportunities to improve? 
Does your team have a healthy amount of discussion in reflection of root causes?
Does your team avoid blaming others when looking at root causes in hindsight? 
Does your team work together to refine their working agreements as they fail forward?
Does your team manage the chaos of life, and client needs, together?
  The Pyramid of Agile Tenets
  This shows a hierarchical structure of Agile team success and what must be in place before teams can perform. At the foundational level, psychological safety must be in place.

# The Four Stages of Team Work
  The Four Stages of Teams: Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing
  Every single team in the world goes through four stages of team work. No one starts by working efficiently with each other. Teams must build and maintain their efficiency.

Reference: https://hr.mit.edu/learning-topics/teams/articles/stages-development
  Forming
  Storming
  Norming
  Performing
  Description: 
During the Forming stage, the team first gets together, and doesn’t have a common way of working established yet, but they meet each other
Tasks:
A team kickoff
Ice breakers
Expectation setting
Feelings: 
Excitement
Belonging
Cheer
Positivity
Confidence
Nervousness
Anxiety
Behaviors: 
Being polite with each other
Questions from team members
Acting excitedly
Uncertainty about the future
Anxiety about their place on the team
  Description:
During the Storming stage, the team starts figuring out how they should be working together, and this happens through talking out disagreements
Tasks:
Defining short-term action items based on goals
Starting work
Deciding how to work together
Feelings: 
Anxiety about whether the team can do what they are set out to do
Anger about the lack of progress
Frustration about the lack of progress
Behaviors:
Arguing about how to work together, and about decisions
Conflict and discussing differences of opinion
Discussing how to start in the work and the goals of the work
Criticizing team mates’ decisions
Questioning the future of the team
  Description:
During the Norming phase, team members resolve their differences, and align in how to work together. They start making agreements in how they should produce the work in collaboration and proceed in the work.
Tasks:

Discussing and building consensus
Collective teamwork
Focusing on aligning goals
Feelings: 
Confidence
Inclusion
Comfort
Behaviors:

Constructive criticism 
Harmoniously working together
Being willing to hear people and work together 
Celebrating team mates for what they bring to the table
  Description:
During the Performing phase, members work efficiently together, and are satisfied in their work together. They work well, and are more aligned than ever in the work. 
Tasks:
Aligning on goals
Planning long-term work
Deepening knowledge
Increasing skills
Increasing accomplishments
Feelings: 
Satisfaction in the work
“Can Do” attitude
Increased confidence
Empowerment
Happiness
Behaviors: 
Getting more work done
More flexibility in the work
Team mates take on multiple roles of responsibility
Team members feel empowered
Appreciation for work and for others

Workshop Summary:
In this workshop, cross-functional teams reflect together about how they can resolve conflict as a unified team while supporting each others' growth.

Conflict is a natural and even necessary part of doing great work in a cross-functional team. This workshop helps teams anticipate conflict and have a plan for what to do when it comes up.
Workshop Goals:
Reflect in how to resolve conflict together as teammates.
Brainstorm contributing factors of conflict.
Hear perspectives from teammates about conflict resolution.
Learn about the relationship between conflict and service leadership.
Workshop Steps to Complete:

Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
Learning how to deal with conflict in a productive way is a huge superpower for any work situation
Conflict is a normal part of working on teams, and many of us feel like conflict is scary or something to be avoided. Learning the skills of conflict resolution and having it driven by teams themselves helps form stronger teammates.
How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Run this early, in the first week or two of a project. Come back to it any time the team feels tension building or wants to reset how it handles disagreements.
Who Owns the Workshop?: Conflict is like Service Leadership. We are all responsible for our own behavior, and we are always looking to support others in their success and growth. The most important thing to remember is that unlike in a context of “work,” in Tech Fleet, no one person can fix or manage conflicts on the team. Our job is to figure out what we can do to make the situation better without blame or shame, even if it means we feel frustrated. We know it can be hard! Please join us for support office hours if you need to talk through a situation.
Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Working Agreements.

# Conflict is Constructive
  Conflict is Constructive
  (10 minutes)

Conflict isn’t something to avoid if teams want to grow. 
Conflict can be good, creative, and generative when we are prepared and hold capacity for healthy conflict.
Through conflict we all must prioritize psychological safety and service leadership with each other. This is the only way for our team to move past instances of conflict: by respecting each other, and understanding each other. 
Anger and frustration are part of life. However, directing anger at another person isn’t healthy. Part of good conflict process is to recognize when we feel a sense of blame, judgment, or anger at someone else and to understand what in us needs attention. We should not suppress our feelings, and we need to own the feelings that we feel as our own feelings, not something someone else made them feel. 
No one can cause you to have a feeling. That doesn’t give us freedom to disregard other people and our impact we have on them, or for other people to disregard their impact on us as teammates.
Let’s watch two videos about conflict and the four stages of team growth.

Workshop Brief: This workshop produces the Statement of Work, the foundational agreement that defines a project's scope, objectives, deliverables, and terms. By aligning with the client on goals, audiences, and problems up front, it sets the shared expectations that keep the whole project from drifting.

Workshop Summary:
This is a workshop teams can run to help build awareness about how cross-functional agile teams operate each sprint. Teams get together and decide how they want to function individually as part of the shared outcomes for a team.

RACI charts are a key Agile team deliverable that breaks down activities and team functions. It shows who’s responsible, who’s accountable, who’s consulted, and who’s informed across the team. Agile teams use this to build shared knowledge and align in their understanding about how they should be working together. Teams create their own RACI charts every sprint. This document shows a template of typical responsibilities based on industry standards.
Workshop Goals:
Educate teams about Agile cross-functional teamwork
Build a shared understanding about who's going to collaborate with whom on sprint teams
Help a team self-organize and build psychological safety by enabling them to make their own decisions about how they get involved


Background

Cross-functional Agile teams are like heist crews: people who get together work towards shared outcomes together and do not stick to only one isolated set of responsibilities. Every time the team plans work, they agree together about who owns what, and who wants to collaborate with whom. This happens every sprint. When you first get together as a new team, each person should identify the desires they are interested in participating and owning for teamwork. You as a self-organized team need to have the power to change this for each person. This allows people to explore new duties they have never done before. The team needs to support people doing work for the first time as Agile teams support each others’ growth together.
Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Review the information provided about Agile teams in the user guide
2. Review the information about typical RACI chart responsibilities per team function
3. Get together as a team and each person will choose their “Hat”, or roles, they want to commit to for the project based on their desires.
4. Everyone builds an avatar character with their desired “Hats”, and voila, you have a cross-functional team outlined in a RACI!
5. Each sprint, you should plan your sprint and re-discuss the individual members’ commitments to the work
Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: RACI charts provide clarity on how team collaboration works on Agile teams. They help everyone on a team build expectations about what they should be doing and how they should be functioning.
How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Build a new RACI every sprint during sprint planning. It is not a one time thing. Update it as people take on different work.
Who Owns the Workshop?:
The Scrum master function on teams owns this deliverable. They must:

Use the template RACI charts to build expectations about functions
Run a sprint planning every sprint where the team builds a new RACI every sprint based on their desired commitments
Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its RACI Charts.
Additional Details:
When to use:
Teams should be building a new RACI chart every sprint through the Sprint Planning activities. Your RACI chart should not just be drafted once. It needs to be adjusted every sprint based on the changing priorities and decisions on the team during the 8 weeks of work. The Scrum Master should make this a habit to keep adjusting the RACI as the weeks go by.

How to involve other teams:
The entire team should get together to review their RACI for the sprint and see whether everyone knows what to expect before the next sprint begins.
Workshop Pitch Statement: A sprint-planning ritual where a cross-functional team decides together who wears which hats (owns which duties) this sprint, captured as a RACI chart of who is responsible, accountable, consulted, and informed.
What You Need Before You Start: Bring the whole team. Have the Agile Handbook material on cross-functional teams open, plus the template RACI charts showing typical responsibilities per function. Set up the FigJam board with the avatar hat-builder and the RACI tables. This is done fresh each sprint during sprint planning.
The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What does it mean to be a cross-functional team that shares duties rather than fixed titles?
2. What are the typical responsibilities per function?
3. Which hats (duties) does each person want to commit to this sprint?
4. Who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed for each activity?
What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with a RACI chart the whole team built for this sprint: each person's committed duties and clear R/A/C/I for every activity. Done well, people stretched into duties they wanted to grow into, and everyone knows what to expect from each other.
Time Needed: About 30 to 45 minutes within sprint planning
Common Pitfalls & Tips: Every activity needs exactly one Accountable; shared accountability disappears. Rebuild the RACI every sprint, not once. And honor the self-organizing spirit: people choose the hats they want to grow into, and the team supports first-timers.
Where to Keep the Output: Keep it with the sprint plan; the Scrum Master updates it each sprint.

Workshop Brief: This workshop produces the team's RACI Charts, the responsibility-assignment matrix that clarifies who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed for each activity (with exactly one person Accountable). Tech Fleet frames it as 'hats' a self-organizing team chooses fresh each sprint.

Workshop Summary:
This template helps teams self-organize in their plan for fixed-timeline projects. Every team should get together and build a forecast based on the anticipated goals. This forecast, known as a Sprint Plan or Project Plan, changes every week, and the Product Owner roles on the team update and maintain this.

A Project Plan outlines each week of work that all team roles are doing, or planning on doing. A sprint team shouldn’t plan everything up front, but rather guess at what’s coming in the later weeks and adjust every week.

Every cross-functional Agile team gets together to decide how they deliver value every sprint. This workshop enables teams to break down their cross-functional work based on the shared outcomes that the project needs to achieve. The team takes the goals and deliverables for a project and determines the 11 week plan based on different functions on the team to make the project a success. In the industry, this deliverable is called a Sprint Plan. In this workshop we call it a Project Plan. It’s maintained every sprint and teams typically plan 2 to 3 sprints ahead so that they can forecast and plan ahead.
Workshop Goals:
Build a forecast of work for the project
Align a full team in knowledge about the upcoming work
Help teams understand what's going on and what's coming up in sprint work
Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Enter the project phase goals as determined by the team
2. Enter the project phase deliverables as determined by the team
3. Everyone get together for an hour: each individual reviews the 11 week breakdown of work that’s provided in the template and maps out additional anticipated activities across functions.
4. Everyone reviews and collaborates together on this activity, and it’s important to develop a consensus.
5. After this workshop, when a team plans a sprint, they will review the project roadmap to identify the planned activities and review them to determine a plan for a two-week chunk of work. During this time, they will commit themselves individually to different kinds of responsibilities they want to take on as people on the team. See the sprint planning workshop template here.
6. Outli
7. Review the pre-determined deliverables per project milestone in Agile product development lifecycles
8. Enter the goals you understand about the project
9. Enter the phase for the project (phase 1, 2, 3, 4, or other)
10. Choose the deliverables your team should work on in your project based on Agile product milestone deliverables provided in this template
11. Enter the project phase deliverables as determined by the team in the space for your project phase
12. The team chooses a pre-determined project plan for phase 1, 2, 3, or 4
13. Everyone reviews the project plan together and determines whether any deliverable outcomes need to change or shift in the project timeline
14. After the project plan is created, a team can run the workshop to outline the sprint goals together. They do this for each sprint and the outcomes of the sprint are based on the project plan.
Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
A project plan(AKA Sprint Plan) is valuable because it:

Aligns teams in work plans across roles
Shows how a team can meet their outcomes
Identifies differences in priority
Helps identify when teams should start work
How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Your project roadmap (AKA Sprint Plan) should not just be drafted once. It needs to be adjusted every week based on the changing priorities and decisions on the team during the 8 weeks of work. The product strategy team should make this a habit to keep adjusting this sprint plan as the weeks go by. They should have the sprint updated by the time they do sprint planning.
Who Owns the Workshop?: The Product Owner function owns the deliverables that come from this workshop, as they own the near-term roadmap orchestration and priorities.
Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Gantt Chart, Sprint Plan, Project Plan, and Project Goals Definition.
Additional Details:
How to involve other teams:
The product strategy team must constantly “own” this deliverable and ensure it’s accurate. They need to talk to the other team roles to ensure that they are bought in with the priorities for each role. This is a conversation and collaboration that takes place weekly. The product strategy team may need to keep this artifact up to date daily. This artifact is used for the basis of sprint planning.

When to Maintain This Deliverable:
A team will be using this deliverable every week to adjust forcast plans. The rest of the team should be using this as a viewable artifact to see what they need to be working on, or identify gaps in priorities that are not already planned.

What to Do After the Workshop:
Every cross-functional Agile team gets together to decide how they deliver value every sprint. This workshop enables teams to break down their cross-functional work based on the shared outcomes that the project needs to achieve. The team takes the goals and deliverables for a project and determines the 11 week plan based on different functions on the team to make the project a success. In the industry, this deliverable is called a Sprint Plan. It’s maintained every sprint and teams typically plan 2 to 3 sprints ahead so that they can forecast and plan ahead.
Workshop Pitch Statement: A whole-team workshop that turns the project's goals into a forecast of work across sprints, so everyone can see what is coming and when, and adjust it weekly.
What You Need Before You Start: Bring the whole team and your project goals from the client intake. Know your project phase (1 to 4) and project type (web platform, discovery, or service design). Open the FigJam board with the deliverables-per-milestone reference and the pre-built phase plans. The Product Owner drafts it, but the whole team reviews and confirms.
The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What are our project goals?
2. What phase and project type are we in?
3. Which deliverables should we produce this phase?
4. Which pre-built phase plan fits us?
5. Do the planned sprint outcomes look right, or do we need to adjust the timeline?
What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with a phase project plan the whole team confirmed: goals, chosen deliverables, and planned outcomes per function across pre-kickoff, four sprints, and hand-off. Done well, everyone can see what is coming, and it is understood as a living forecast, not a fixed promise.
Time Needed: About 60 to 90 minutes to build, then updated weekly
Common Pitfalls & Tips: Do not plan everything up front in detail; forecast the later weeks and adjust weekly. Remember the lifecycle is non-linear, so milestones repeat and overlap rather than run in a straight line. The Product Owner keeps it current and uses it to run sprint planning.
Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam; the Product Owner updates it weekly, before each sprint planning.

Workshop Brief: This workshop produces the Project Plan, along with a Gantt-style timeline, sprint plan, and project goals. A project plan lays out phases, milestones, and outcomes across the work, but in agile it is a living forecast that adjusts weekly, not a fixed waterfall schedule.

Workshop Summary: Products aren’t just made from ideas. They take a lot of coordination, research, decisions, and negotiations to make happen. Teams in the world who focus on their audience’s problems can transform their teamwork into a larger long-term map of success. Teams must maintain and update the deliverables that showcase the long-term outcomes over time as they learn new insights in research. This workshop helps a team to outline how to take a team’s current understanding of the problems in their audience’s current state, identify the goals, and create the maps for long-term release outcomes that they need to follow while performing UX, product, or development work.
Workshop Goals:
Identify your known audiences
Identify problems you think your audiences experience today in current state of the world
Prioritize the problems you want to focus on now and later.
Communicate the problems you identify as goals, value, unique advantage, and outcomes in a vision for near-term and long-term releases.
Organize the work outcomes into themes and chunk the backlog work into feasible work items.
Develop a roadmap plan for the next year that you can maintain.
Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Enter the components of product vision you want to focus on for yourself
2. Your target audiences
3. Your personal opportunities and problems
4. Your business goals
5. Your value you bring to the world when you solve the problems you want to solve
6. What makes you unique as a business compared to others in the market space, and how you differentiate the business
7. The barriers and risks that may get in your way to success in the product release, and how you will mitigate them
8. The “costs” of money, time, and energy involved
9. Your KPI’s and measures of success
10. Your scope of outcomes to achieve based on the problems you want to solve
11. Prioritize the problems in a priority matrix
12. Pick the most important 5 problems for you to work on near-term, and choose them for your “MVP #1 Release” for the vision
13. Create vision boards for your upcoming releases based on the problems you’ve prioritized:
14. “MVP #1”, also known as “Problems to solve and validate first”
15. “MMP”, also known as “Problems to solve at market”
16. Create your scope of outcomes to achieve based on the value and problems to solve for each release
17. Create epics, features, and tasks based on the scope of outcomes
18. Create your roadmap
19. Populate your backlog with the tasks related to features and epics
Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
A vision, scope, and roadmap for products and services is valuable because:

It breaks down larger goals into smaller, more accomplishable results
It helps you communicate language around your goals, needs, value delivery, and action items.
It helps you determine what your team should focus on now and later, and organizes work for the entire team.
How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: You should revisit the vision and roadmap on a regular basis. This will help you keep track of items you work on throughout the year and pivot when you need to.
Who Owns the Workshop?: The product owner and product manager own these deliverables for the purposes of release management and backlog management.
Expected Outcomes:
Problems and opportunities that audiences experience
KPI’s for your release
Release-Level vision for MVP and MMP
Release-Level scope of work for MVP and MMP
Epics, features, and tasks list for MVP and MMP
Release roadmap
Backlog with task tickets and appropriately categorized epics / features
Additional Details:
Where to keep it:
Keep it in Figjam, or some other place where you can keep it over time
Workshop Pitch Statement: A workshop where the team turns its audiences' prioritized problems into release-level vision boards and a clear scope of outcomes for what to build now (MVP) and later (MMP).
What You Need Before You Start: Bring the product owner and product manager (they own it) and the whole team, plus your known audiences and the problems you assume they face. Set up FigJam with the vision components, the priority matrices, and the vision-board templates. Best once discovery is underway; revisit regularly.
The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What are our audiences, problems, goals, value, unique advantage, barriers, costs, and KPIs?
2. Which problems matter most now versus later?
3. What are our top few problems for the first release?
4. What is the release vision (MVP and MMP) per audience?
5. What scope of outcomes will each release achieve?
What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with a release-level vision board per audience for MVP and MMP, a prioritized problem set, and a scope of outcomes per release. Done well, everyone can see exactly what value each release delivers to each audience, and the vision is understood as living, not final.
Time Needed: A substantial session, then revisited regularly
Common Pitfalls & Tips: These are assumptions, not truths yet; you validate them in research. Make one vision board per audience per release on purpose, so the value stays specific. And treat the vision as never final; revisit it as you learn.
Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam; the product owner and manager maintain it.

# For Each Audience: Prioritize the Problems
  For Each Audience: Prioritize the Problems
  Take your use cases you’ve identified on the first section and prioritize them for each audience
  How do you know which problems to solve first?
In short: you don't, and no one does. It's all just a guess and a judgment call based on what you know. You could get the guess wrong, and Agile is built for quick adjustments when you get it wrong. One needs to embrace this lifestyle in requirements work for Agile teams. You will constantly be guessing which is the correct way to go. "Continuous improvement" all the way. You can use tools like prioritization matrices to rank problems to solve and decide which ones to solve first. The rest is up to what the team decides to put into their release-level vision, and what they learn after they deliver iterations towards the release.

"Must Should Could Won't" Prioritization matrix (AKA "MoSCoW Matrix")
The "Must Should Could Won't" priority matrix helps teams quickly decide which items to prioritize. It helps you quickly place things into categories based on different criteria:

# Create your Release Vision and Scope
  Make One Vision Board Per Release, Per Audience

You’ve now identified the key problems, goals, value, barriers, and unique advantage about your product or service. You are ready to put together a release-level vision board! The release is made up of many problems to solve. In the sections below, write the components of the vision board based on the input you provided in part 1. Only worry about the first release (MVP #1) and the market-ready release (MMP).

You should make one vision board per audience, per release. 

For instance: if you have two target audiences, you will be making 4 vision boards: MVP for Audience 1, MMP for Audience 1, MVP for Audience 2, and MMP for Audience 2.

You may be asking yourself, "Why? This seems like more work..." Yes it is. It is very purposeful. This approach is helpful to specify what exact value you're delivering for each audience each time you release. Without this approach, you may not communicate the exact problems you're solving, or value you're delivering, for each audience. It's best to proceed one audience, one release at a time.

# How to Build a Backlog of Work
  Group your Release-Level Scope into Epics and Features
  Epics and features are like the containers and drawers in your kitchen:
Epics are like your kitchen drawers and cabinets

  With your release-level vision, scope, and roadmap, you can start populating your backlog and working towards the work to be delivered for project teams. This doesn’t happen all at once, but rather incrementally over time. Each sprint, you should be producing new requirements and task-level details that are coordinated with the rest of the team functions. Workshop Brief: This workshop produces the release Vision Boards, Release-level Scope, Epics and Features, and Roadmap. A vision board (Roman Pichler's tool) captures the vision, target group, needs, key features, and business goals; scope draws the line around what a release will and will not include. Both stay living as the team learns.

Workshop Summary: You may think that someone dictates how a team should work in Agile. After all, we have all of the rules written in Scrum, right? Don't all Agile teams operate the same? They tell us what meetings to do, when to do them, and how to do them. This is a misconception. Agile teams govern themselves and own their own process together. Everyone on the team, even the interns, even the apprentices, should have a say in how they work together. This is a principle called self-organization, and it's crucial to build on Agile teams. In order for them to do their best work, they must be handed the keys to ownership of the process. A team process looks different on every team. At its core, it's a summarized agreement for how a team wants to work across functions to get work done. The process is visualized in a flow chart so that everyone can understand how work gets done. When the team takes retrospectives and discusses how to change their process with working agreements, they should update this team process flow chart to ensure it's accurately depicting how the team operates.
Workshop Goals:
Learn about the Scrum method of Agile
Learn about how agile teams use a tool called a Kanban Board to manage a backlog of work and the statuses of work
Build your own team process in a flow chart
Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Product strategy duties
2. Notion space and documentation of the product
3. Agile product development and milestones
4. Assumption forming and assumption testing
5. Building a process that works for your team
6. Implementing process in the kanban board on Notion
Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: Agile team process maps are valuable because they align a whole team in their understanding of how work happens together. When new team members join, they can be onboarded faster. When someone is uncertain what to do next, they can point to the team process and build clarity. It helps a team operate in a smooth fashion.
How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Build the first version at the start of a project. Update it whenever the team changes how it works, usually after a sprint retro.
Who Owns the Workshop?: The Product Operations function maintains the team process. This is usually handled in Scrum teams by the Scrum Master role or the Product Owner role.
Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Prioritized Backlog Tasks, Refined Backlog, Kanban Board Statuses, and Team Process Map.

# Problem Solving and Assumptions
  Assumption Forming and Testing
  This is what happens when you don’t document requirements, and run with assumptions that are not validated

  # Section 2
  Teams are making a lot of assumptions. In fact, every decision a team makes is an assumption. They assume they're making the right decision for the business or for the users. The assumptions could be justified with a lot of research, or backed by estimated guesses, but they are assumptions nonetheless.
Nothing will ever be verified to be true or false until your entire audience uses something and you get enough data that's representative of the population and statistically significant.
Agile teams release early and often, and they continuously improve by testing their assumptions and refining their vision. Over time, they deliver more value to users and validate more assumptions. This is cyclical in nature; every time something gets delivered, new assumptions form, and the team should keep validating every new assumption being made.

# Agile

# Milestones and the Development Lifecycle
  Requirements deliverables based on assumptions

Proto-personas
When first starting to gather requirements, teams can start with assumptions about their users with Proto-Personas. This is a common Agile UX deliverable and involves making personas based on your assumptions about users (no research necessary). Traditional personas are delivered after research, but proto-personas are only made with guesses. The purpose of this is to help a team align in the assumptions they are making about users, and to validate them early and refine. Over time, the proto-personas become more refined and less assumptive, turning into "personas".

Vision and Scope
The vision boards should NOT only be delivered once and forgotten about (like with Waterfall processes). Every time a team learns about the business or users, the vision must be reviewed and refined in order to adjust the assumptions being made. Sometimes this causes big changes in the vision and sometimes a team's assumptions were correct. This is to be expected when delivering things iteratively, and teams should adopt the mindset that the "vision is never final", only refined over time.

User stories and acceptance criteria
User stories and acceptance criteria operate on decisions that are made by teams, which are also, you guessed it, ASSUMPTIONS! Teams don't know for certain whether this will meet the audience's needs and need to deliver quickly or test before delivering to check the assumptions. It's important for user stories and acceptance criteria to be small chunks of work so that this process can happen quickly.

Release plans
Your release plan assumes you're going to deliver things when you think you are going to deliver. As the state of the world changes, and team or user needs change, so should the release plans. Teams who check their assumptions early and often must review and refine release plans constantly. This becomes a daily or weekly upkeep for product owners or product managers.

  # Kanban Roles
    Kanban Roles
    “The Heist Team”
    There are no roles specified for the Kanban process! Your team is a “team doing work”. Each person can pitch in to manage the backlog, do work, report on progress, run meetings, or anything else that the team needs to do. This method relies heavily on a self-organized team to build and live their own process together.

  # Kanban Process
    Kanban Process
    “To Do / Doing / Done”
    At its basic level, Kanban method helps teams track three statuses of work: To Do, Doing, and Done. Yes that’s it! A team simply gets work ready with requirements, starts the work when they are ready, and delivers the work when they are done. They do not plan when work will happen, they simply make judgments about the priorities of work based on the order of items in the backlog

WHAT IS THIS?
STEPS TO RUN THE WORKSHOP
You may think that someone dictates how a team should work in Agile. After all, we have all of the rules written in Scrum, right? Don't all Agile teams operate the same? They tell us what meetings to do, when to do them, and how to do them. This is a misconception. Agile teams govern themselves and own their own process together. Everyone on the team, even the interns, even the apprentices, should have a say in how they work together. This is a principle called self-organization, and it's crucial to build on Agile teams. In order for them to do their best work, they must be handed the keys to ownership of the process. A team process looks different on every team. At its core, it's a summarized agreement for how a team wants to work across functions to get work done. The process is visualized in a flow chart so that everyone can understand how work gets done. When the team takes retrospectives and discusses how to change their process with working agreements, they should update this team process flow chart to ensure it's accurately depicting how the team operates.
OUTCOMES OF THE WORKSHOP
Team process map to show how work gets done on the team that the team will maintain
HOW OFTEN SHOULD IT BE UPDATED?
Your team should be maintaining the team process whenever it needs to change. This will change with the working agreements and retrospectives.
WHY IS IT VALUABLE?
Agile team process maps are valuable because they align a whole team in their understanding of how work happens together. When new team members join, they can be onboarded faster. When someone is uncertain what to do next, they can point to the team process and build clarity. It helps a team operate in a smooth fashion.
GOALS OF THE WORKSHOP
Learn about the Scrum method of Agile
Learn about how agile teams use a tool called a Kanban Board to manage a backlog of work and the statuses of work
Build your own team process in a flow chart
WHO OWNS THIS DELIVERABLE?
The Product Operations function maintains the team process. This is usually handled in Scrum teams by the Scrum Master role or the Product Owner role.
WHERE SHOULD THIS BE KEPT?
Keep it in Figjam, or some other place where you can keep it over time
Workshop Brief: This workshop produces the Team Process Map and the Kanban Board Statuses. A Kanban board tracks work through statuses (To Do, Doing, Done) with work-in-progress limits to keep work flowing; the process map is the self-organizing team's own picture of how work moves from idea to done.

Workshop Summary: Sprint Goals are created every sprint before the sprint begins. Teams get together and review their plans to outline the outcomes they want to achieve. Then they break down the outcomes into steps to complete and considerations. The people on the team commit themselves to the work so that they can determine themselves how they want to be involved: responsible, accountable, consulted, or informed.
Workshop Goals:
Create the plan of the shared outcomes for a sprint across a cross-functional teams
Assign people to work before the sprint begins
Set the sprint RACI chart
Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Review the work that your team planned from the project plan above.
2. Copy the items from the planned sprint into the space where sprint outcomes go
3. Have everyone on the team who is committing to work add themselves to sticky notes to commit to the sprint
4. Team discusses the steps to complete each task
5. Team discusses any additional requirements or considerations that are needed to complete the work
6. The team assigns themselves either responsible, accountable, consulted, or informed for the work.
7. The team re-edits their RACI hats for the sprint and drops their new RACI hats on their character.
Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
Sprint goals are valuable because they:
Set a plan for the sprint
Give clarity in who’s doing the work 
Give clarity in how the work will be done
How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: You should create a new sprint goal set every sprint.
Who Owns the Workshop?: The Scrum Master duty on the team will own this deliverable alongside the product owner and the whole team who contributes to the input of the planned work.
Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Sprint Goals.
Additional Details:
When to use:
A team will be using this deliverable before every sprint begins. The rest of the team should be using this as a viewable artifact to see what they need to be working on, or identify gaps in priorities that are not already planned.
Workshop Pitch Statement: A short, recurring session where the team turns the sprint's slice of the project plan into one clear goal, broken into steps with owners.
What You Need Before You Start: Bring the whole team and your project plan; it sets each sprint's planned outcomes. Do this at the start of each sprint, during sprint planning. Open the FigJam board with the sprint goal and steps template.
The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What outcomes does the project plan call for this sprint?
2. What is our single sprint goal?
3. What steps does it break into?
4. Who owns each step?
What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with one clear sprint goal, the outcomes it covers, and steps with owners the whole team agreed to. Done well, the goal is focused and attainable, and everyone knows their part.
Time Needed: About 30 to 60 minutes at the start of each sprint
Common Pitfalls & Tips: Keep it to a single objective; a sprint goal is one focus, not a laundry list. Base it on the project plan's outcomes, and keep it visible so the team can check progress in the daily standup. The goal provides focus while leaving flexibility in exactly how you reach it.
Where to Keep the Output: Keep it with the sprint plan in FigJam, and revisit it in the daily standup.

Workshop Brief: This workshop produces Sprint Goals, the single objective for a sprint (per the Scrum Guide) that gives the team focus and a target to measure progress against, while leaving flexibility in exactly how the team gets there.

Workshop Summary: The team works with an Agile Coach to set up and organize its backlog. Together they turn ideas and requirements into user stories and task tickets, add acceptance criteria, and put the work in order in a tool like Notion, so the team always knows what to pick up next.
Workshop Goals:
Turn requirements into clear user stories and tasks
Write acceptance criteria so everyone knows when work is done
Put the backlog in priority order
Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: A messy backlog slows a team down and causes confusion about what to build. A clear, ordered backlog lets the team focus on the most important work and move faster with less back and forth.
How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Set up the backlog early, then keep it up to date. The team should refine and reorder it during every sprint.
Who Owns the Workshop?: The Product Operations function owns this workshop and is responsible for running it with the team.
Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Acceptance Criteria and Prioritized Backlog Tasks.
Additional Details: When to use: set it up at the start and keep it going through every sprint.
Workshop Pitch Statement: A workshop where the team turns its release scope into an organized backlog of epics, features, and tasks, then builds a roadmap and populates the backlog to guide the build.
What You Need Before You Start: Bring the product owner and manager (they own release and backlog management) and your release-level vision and scope from the Vision and Scope workshop. Set up FigJam with the epic, feature, and task organizer and the roadmap. Revisit regularly as priorities shift.
The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What epics and features come out of our release scope?
2. What tasks make up each feature?
3. What does our release roadmap look like?
4. What goes into the backlog, and in what order?
What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with a backlog of epics, features, and tasks organized from the release scope, a roadmap, and a populated, prioritized backlog ready to write requirements against. Done well, the work ladders directly up to the release vision, and the team knows what to build next.
Time Needed: A substantial session, then maintained regularly
Common Pitfalls & Tips: Organize work into themes (epics), then features, then small tasks that fit the INVEST idea. Keep the backlog prioritized at all times. And treat the roadmap as living; adjust it as you learn.
Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam and your backlog tool; the product team maintains it.

# For Each Audience: Prioritize the Problems
  For Each Audience: Prioritize the Problems
  Take your use cases you’ve identified on the first section and prioritize them for each audience
  How do you know which problems to solve first?
In short: you don't, and no one does. It's all just a guess and a judgment call based on what you know. You could get the guess wrong, and Agile is built for quick adjustments when you get it wrong. One needs to embrace this lifestyle in requirements work for Agile teams. You will constantly be guessing which is the correct way to go. "Continuous improvement" all the way. You can use tools like prioritization matrices to rank problems to solve and decide which ones to solve first. # Create your Release Vision and Scope
  Make One Vision Board Per Release, Per Audience

You’ve now identified the key problems, goals, value, barriers, and unique advantage about your product or service. You are ready to put together a release-level vision board! The release is made up of many problems to solve. In the sections below, write the components of the vision board based on the input you provided in part 1. Only worry about the first release (MVP #1) and the market-ready release (MMP).

You should make one vision board per audience, per release. 

For instance: if you have two target audiences, you will be making 4 vision boards: MVP for Audience 1, MMP for Audience 1, MVP for Audience 2, and MMP for Audience 2.

You may be asking yourself, "Why? This seems like more work..." Yes it is. It is very purposeful. This approach is helpful to specify what exact value you're delivering for each audience each time you release. Without this approach, you may not communicate the exact problems you're solving, or value you're delivering, for each audience. It's best to proceed one audience, one release at a time.

This doesn’t happen all at once, but rather incrementally over time. Workshop Brief: This workshop produces a refined, Prioritized Backlog and its Acceptance Criteria. Backlog refinement keeps the to-do list clear, sized, and ordered; acceptance criteria are the agreed conditions (often given-when-then) that define when each item is done.

Workshop Summary:
This is a sprint retrospective template for Agile cross-functional teams to reflect in their previous sprint, measure their agility, and take action on the process changes they want to make as a team.

A sprint retrospective is the most important meeting for a sprint team. The full team, all apprentices and co-leads, get together after every sprint and hold a safe space to reflect on their last sprint.
Workshop Goals:
Every sprint, Agile teams should get together to reflect in their work:

Celebrate what went well
Measure how far they have progressed
Discuss what they want to improve about their own process together
Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Do the 4 L's: what did the team like, learn, lack, and long for? 
2. Who gave great service leadership? 
3. What deliverables did you complete? 
4. Rank your agile maturity scores
5. Identify action items and make plans for improvement
Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
A sprint retrospective is valuable because:

It allows room for people to speak freely about what process changes they want to make.
It holds space for teams to continuously improve after reflection and collective agreement.
It reinforces self-organization, putting the success of the team in the hands of the team itself, and no one outside the team.
How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Hold a retro at the end of every sprint. It is one of the most important team meetings, so do not skip it.
Who Owns the Workshop?:
People playing the Scrum Master role own this deliverable. They must:

Facilitate this meeting as Scrum Master role
Document action items
Send out the summary after
Update working agreements
Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Sprint Retro Action Items and Agile Maturity Measurements.
Additional Details:
When to use:
After every sprint, the team should get together to hold a sprint retrospective.

How to involve other teams:
Get together after every sprint
Part 1: what did you like, what did you learn, what did you lack, and what did you long for?
Part 2: Identify action items for how to change process on the team, and brainstorm together about how to change it, and assign the person who’s going to own the outcomes of the changes (it could be anyone on the team)
Part 3: Measure your team’s levels of agility by answering the questions on the workshop

Everyone on the team, including apprentices and co-leads, needs to participate in retrospectives. The team owns their own process and they must participate to feel the full stake of ownership in it.
Workshop Pitch Statement: The team's most important recurring meeting: a safe space after every sprint to reflect, celebrate wins, and agree concrete changes to how the team works.
What You Need Before You Start: Bring the whole team, including apprentices and co-leads; everyone participates. Set up the FigJam board with the 4 Ls retro and the action-items table. The product strategy team facilitates it as Scrum Master. Do it after every sprint.
The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What did we like, learn, lack, and long for this sprint?
2. Who showed great service leadership, and why?
3. What should we change about our process?
4. Who owns each change, and does it update our working agreements?
What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with honest reflections, service-leadership recognition, and a set of owned action items for improving your process, with working agreements updated. Done well, everyone spoke freely, and the team, not anyone outside it, owns the changes.
Time Needed: About 60 minutes after each sprint
Common Pitfalls & Tips: Keep it a safe space; this reinforces self-organization, so no one outside the team drives the changes. Turn reflections into owned action items, or nothing actually changes. Send the summary and update the working agreements afterward.
Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam; update the working agreements and send a summary afterward.

  WHAT IS THIS?
  HOW TO RUN THE WORKSHOP
  Agile maturity measurements help a self-organized team measure how agile their operations are. These are based on the different facets of the Agile Manifesto and the steps to create self-actualized agile teams.
  Get together after every sprint
Hold a retrospective workshop 
Hold the Agile Maturity measurements workshop to Measure how often a team:
Followed the Agile Manifesto
Interacted with individuals to figure out work over making a perfect plan before starting work
Delivered working UX results to clients and to users to figure out their priorities through feedback
Collaborated with each other, with users, and with clients to define requirements over making contracted agreements.
Followed the Agile tenets of strong Agile teams
Created a psychologically safe space for voices on the team
Acted as service leaders to each other (apprentices and co-leads)
Organized themselves and made their own governing decisions through consensus
Failed fast and continuously improved
Iterated on their value delivery
  WHY IS IT VALUABLE?
  Measuring agile maturity is valuable because:
It helps a team self-heal when they are performing waterfall practices instead of agile practices.
It helps identify potential areas of improvement for team operations.
It creates a safe space for the team to hold psychological safety and be vulnerable with their potential issues as a team.

Workshop Brief: This workshop produces Sprint Retro Action Items. A retrospective is the recurring meeting where a team reflects and commits to concrete improvements; Tech Fleet uses the 4 Ls format (liked, learned, lacked, longed for) and turns reflections into owned action items, the engine of continuous improvement.

Workshop Summary:
This is a workshop template to help cross-functional Agile teams develop their own principles of self-organization known as a working agreement. There are multiple working agreements across different areas on teams. These change whenever the team takes a retrospective on work and agrees to change the way they work.

Working agreements are an Agile deliverable that act as a set of guidelines and expectations established by a team or group to govern how they will work together effectively. The team changes them as their team matures over time. Working agreements are commonly used in various contexts, including Agile and Scrum development teams, but they can be applied to any group or project where people need to work together cohesively.
Workshop Goals:
Define team expectations in how a whole team approaches work together
Collect perspectives and desires from the team in how they want to work together across functions
Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Review the information provided about Agile teams in the user guide
2. Answer the questions as a team for how you will abide by the Agile tenets together:
3. How will your team build psychological safety?
4. How will your team build service leadership?
5. How will your team build self-organization?
6. How will your team build continuous improvement?
7. How will your team deal with and resolve conflict?
8. How will your team handle pivoting?
9. How will your team handle communication?
10. What else do you want to agree to?
Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: Working agreements provide expectations and guidelines for teams who need to work together across functions. These agreements help create a shared understanding of how team members will interact, communicate, and collaborate to achieve their goals.
How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Working agreements should be updated as teams go through sprint retros and learn how they want to change their process together.
Who Owns the Workshop?: The Scrum Master role owns this deliverable and facilitates it with the team. They get the team together to build a collective consensus and take action on listing out agreements that the team wants to note. The Scrum Master maintains these working agreements as they change after every retro.
Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Psychological Safety Plan.
Additional Details:
When to use:
The collective team, led by the Scrum Master role, should build a consensus about working agreements before the project begins. This should happen during the first two weeks of a project phase, and they adjust after each sprint retro.

How to involve other teams:
The entire team should get together to build their working agreements together so that they commit to them collectively. Each time the agreements change, the full team should review and approve them before enacting new working agreements.
Workshop Pitch Statement: A session where a new team writes its own ground rules, deciding together how it will build psychological safety, share leadership, self-organize, improve, and handle conflict and change.
What You Need Before You Start: Bring the whole team, with the Scrum Master to facilitate. Have the Agile Handbook's material on strong agile teams open (the tenets and the agility checklists), and set up the FigJam board with an agreement section for each agile tenet. This works best in the first two weeks of a phase.
The Core Questions You're Answering: How will our team build: 1. psychological safety, 2. service leadership, 3. self-organization, 4. continuous improvement? And how will we: 5. resolve conflict, 6. handle pivoting, 7. communicate, 8. collaborate across functions, and 9. move past storming?
What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with a set of written agreements the whole team shaped and committed to, covering each agile tenet plus conflict, pivoting, and communication. Done well, they are the team's own words, not a template, and everyone genuinely buys in.
Time Needed: About 60 to 90 minutes
Common Pitfalls & Tips: These are living; revisit and update them after every sprint retro as the team matures. Build them together so people commit collectively, and re-approve as a full team when they change. Ground each agreement in the agile tenet it supports.
Where to Keep the Output: Keep them in the team's shared space; the Scrum Master maintains them and the team revisits after each retro.

  The Scrum Master role owns this deliverable and facilitates it with the team. They get the team together to build a collective consensus and take action on listing out agreements that the team wants to note. The Scrum Master maintains these working agreements as they change after every retro.
  WHEN DO TEAMS USE THIS?
  The collective team, led by the Scrum Master role, should build a consensus about working agreements before the project begins. This should happen during the first two weeks of a project phase, and they adjust after each sprint retro.
  HOW OFTEN SHOULD IT BE UPDATED?
  Working agreements should be updated as teams go through sprint retros and learn how they want to change their process together.

# Building Agile Teams that Perform
  The Basic Tenets of Agile Team Building
  Measuring the Agile Tenets
  Agile team strength is like a garden: you have to maintain agility and pick out the weeds to ensure health and growth of your team. How teams do this is open to the person owning the product, and the scrum master. 

Here are some key points to determine levels of self-organization, psychological safety, servant leadership, iterative value delivery, and continuous improvement.
  To measure Agility, teams must look at the components of what makes an Agile team agile: self-organization, psychological safety, servant leadership, iterative value, and continuous improvement. Here’s a set of checklists you can use to determine your team’s current state of agility.
  Self-organization: 

Allow the day-to-day people doing the work to make decisions themselves, instead of the people leading the team, and let the team carry out their own work in the way they want, or think is best
  Psychological Safety:

Build the sense of safety and belonging throughout the team:
Make every member of the team feel like they have room to speak their mind
Actively listen when others have things to say, and make team feel like their voice matters
Give the room for people to bring their own personalities and unique capabilities to the table in the way THEY want to do so
Allow room for team mates to challenge the status quo, and experiment with new ways of working
Encourage failing “fast”, i.e. failure and quick reflection and quick adjustment based on what the team thinks they should do
Let them take the risks that THEY decide to take, that could lead to failure or disaster, for the purposes of allowing them to build up decision making prowess

Workshop Name: Scenario-Based Problem Statement Generation Workshop Template
Workshop Summary: The team learns how to write clear problem statements based on real situations users face today. Starting from what is happening in the world right now, the team describes the problem, the user's needs and goals, and turns those into user stories the team can act on.
Workshop Goals:
Learn how to write problem statements from real user situations
Describe user needs and goals in plain language
Turn problems into user stories the team can build from
Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Dump the unrefined problems
2. Break into aspects
3. Refine the aspects
4. Break the aspects into Formal Problem Statements (why, what, who, when)
5. Create Problem Checklist (user goal, user need, consequences, user story) for each Formal Problem Statement
6. Prioritize the problems to put back into the Vision and Scope
Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: Teams waste time when they jump to solutions before they understand the problem. Writing clear problem statements keeps the team focused on what users actually need, so the work solves a real problem.
How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Do this during discovery whenever the team is trying to understand a new problem. Come back to it as you learn more from research.
Who Owns the Workshop?: The Product Management function owns this workshop and is responsible for running it with the team.
Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Problem Statements, Problem Checklists, and User Story Statements.
Additional Details: When to use: during discovery, after sprints begin, when the team is deciding what to solve.
Workshop Pitch Statement: A workshop that turns a pile of assumed problems into sharp, root-cause problem statements, problem checklists, and user stories the team can build against.
What You Need Before You Start: Bring the team and every problem you assume about the current state, per audience (from discovery or your own hunches). Set up the FigJam board with the problem-dump space and the breakdown tables. Best during discovery and requirements.
The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What problems do we assume, for each audience?
2. What are the raw aspects (situations) behind each?
3. What is the root of each, found with the 5 Whys?
4. Who faces it, when, and why does it matter, and what user goal, need, and consequences follow?
What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with formal problem statements (root + aspect + who + when + why), a problem checklist for each (goal, need, consequences to avoid), and a user story for each. Done well, they describe real problems, never solutions, and give the team something concrete to prioritize.
Time Needed: A substantial amount of working sessions over the course of a sprint
Common Pitfalls & Tips: Describe problems, not solutions; the board warns of this trap repeatedly (a goal and a need are not a solution). Use the 5 Whys to reach the real root. And write one audience per checklist, so problems can be prioritized cleanly later.
Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam and refine the problem statements constantly as you learn.

# Section 6
  Assumption Forming and Testing
  This is what happens when you don’t document requirements, and run with assumptions that are not validated
  Assumptions and Requirements
  Teams are making a lot of assumptions. In fact, every decision a team makes is an assumption. They assume they're making the right decision for the business or for the users. The assumptions could be justified with a lot of research, or backed by estimated guesses, but they are assumptions nonetheless.
Nothing will ever be verified to be true or false until your entire audience uses something and you get enough data that's representative of the population and statistically significant.
Agile teams release early and often, and they continuously improve by testing their assumptions and refining their vision. Over time, they deliver more value to users and validate more assumptions. This is cyclical in nature; every time something gets delivered, new assumptions form, and the team should keep validating every new assumption being made.
  Credit: Google Ventures (Google Design Sprint)
  Requirements deliverables based on assumptions

Proto-personas
When first starting to gather requirements, teams can start with assumptions about their users with Proto-Personas. This is a common Agile UX deliverable and involves making personas based on your assumptions about users (no research necessary). Traditional personas are delivered after research, but proto-personas are only made with guesses. The purpose of this is to help a team align in the assumptions they are making about users, and to validate them early and refine. Over time, the proto-personas become more refined and less assumptive, turning into "personas".

Vision and Scope
The vision boards should NOT only be delivered once and forgotten about (like with Waterfall processes). Every time a team learns about the business or users, the vision must be reviewed and refined in order to adjust the assumptions being made. Sometimes this causes big changes in the vision and sometimes a team's assumptions were correct. This is to be expected when delivering things iteratively, and teams should adopt the mindset that the "vision is never final", only refined over time.

User stories and acceptance criteria
User stories and acceptance criteria operate on decisions that are made by teams, which are also, you guessed it, ASSUMPTIONS! Teams don't know for certain whether this will meet the audience's needs and need to deliver quickly or test before delivering to check the assumptions. It's important for user stories and acceptance criteria to be small chunks of work so that this process can happen quickly.

Release plans
Your release plan assumes you're going to deliver things when you think you are going to deliver. As the state of the world changes, and team or user needs change, so should the release plans. Teams who check their assumptions early and often must review and refine release plans constantly. This becomes a daily or weekly upkeep for product owners or product managers.

# Section 8
  Solution vs. Problem vs. Need vs. Goal
  “We want you to draw 7 red lines, 4 with blue ink, 3 with transparent ink. Can you do it?”
  How do you know the solution that a stakeholder brings you will meet user needs? How do you know it's solving the right problem to begin with?
You don't!
  A solution is something that is assumed HOW to solve a problem.

A problem describes a SITUATIONAL USE CASE that’s happening in the current state of the world, describing something lacking or missing in the state of the world. Users experience problems because of how they interact with the world.   A user goal describes THE OUTCOME a user is trying to achieve.  A business goal describes THE OUTCOME a business is trying to achieve.

A user need describes basic human-level expectation and desire based on the problem to be solved.   A business need describes expectation and desires for a business based on the problem to be solved.  A technical need describes requirement from a technical standpoint based on the problem to be solved.

# RESEARCHING THE CURRENT STATE OF THE WORLD
  Researching the Current State of the World
  Teams must understand: 
How something works today
How users behave
How users expect 
How users think
How they experience the problems 
The ecosystem in which the problems live

UX research Methods
Contextual inquiries - Walk alongside a user as they go through activities in "a day in the life", ask them questions
Ethnography - Observe things in the world and take note
Interviews - Ask people questions in conversation
Card sorts - Understand how people would rank or categorize things
Surveys - Ask people questions asynchronously
Web analytics audits - Look at web analytics to see how audiences are behaving online
Usability tests - Measure how successfully people do or understand something
Concept tests - Test a concept idea with potential audiences

Teams must also understand the market: 

Market size
Teams should understand the state of the market and the opportunities for growth within the market. This comes with analyzing the total market cap of products that are similar to the product being built. Tools online offer abilities to look at market research and understand the market they're trying to enter. This is important in order to understand how "saturated" the market is before moving too far ahead with their work. If the market has too many other competitors that try to solve the same problems, then the team needs to strategize on how their product is going to uniquely provide value.

Market segmentation
Within markets there may be sub-categories of products that specifically solve problems. Teams should understand where exactly their product fits into the market in order to form good assumptions about where their product fits in.

Direct and indirect competitors
There may be other products on the market that try to solve the same or similar problems. Vetting them is key to deciding how to differentiate your product from others. There could be products that have similar features and similar customers as yours, or products that indirectly solve the problems you are trying to solve. Teams should document and analyze all of this before moving ahead with their vision.

Unique selling proposition / competitive advantage
If a product doesn't bring something uniquely valuable to the table, there's a low likelihood that users will abandon existing products and convert to the one your team's building. Refining a unique selling proposition takes analysis of the market and its competitors to understand what none of them do well.

  Finding the Root of Problems
  When a problem is defined, it may not be the root of the problem. Keep asking “Why is this a problem” to find the most meaningful root problem.
  People don’t have enough resources and it causes them to get sick
  Enter the problem
  Not having enough food impairs your brain activity
  Keep digging: Why is this a problem?
  People may not be able to function in society
  Keep digging: Why is this a problem?
  People may be more likely to resort to stealing 
People may not be able to have as much choice in their own lives
  Keep digging: Why is this a problem?
  So: What is the root problem?
  Anatomy of a problem statement

Problem statements have several parts:

What is the root problem?
The root of the problem can be tricky to describe, or uncover. It takes research and understanding your audiences to be able to do so. Once you have a good understanding, the root problem should be described in one sentence. See the other lessons in this section for details about how to uncover the root problems, and aspects of the problem.

Which audience experiences the problem?
This describes your target audiences that experience the problem. You must have a good understanding about the audiences you are building for first, but this can be a guess (an assumption) before you validate with further work.
When and where is it a problem for users?
Describe the situations and scenarios where this comes up for users. Doing this helps others understand how to empathize with the user and understand the context in which they experience the problem.

Why is it important to solve?
There's a quote from a movie: "ABC: Always Be Closing". Always be closing when describing your problem statements. Provide justifications why the problem is worth solving, or else. In team discussions, if you do not have a good reason why it's important to solve this problem for users, no one on your team, and especially no one outside your team, will be bought in to building it. Why spend time and money on solutions if it's is not worth solving? ABC!
