Each problem statement has a corresponding problem checklist. Each problem statement / problem checklist has a corresponding user story statement.

Audience
Only write one audience per problem checklist. If two or more audiences face the same problem, then write different problem checklists for each audience. You should do this so that they can properly be prioritized in your vision and scope (see the next week's lessons for more). You will use this section later when you generate your user story statements.

Problem statement
Take your problem statement that you formed and drop it here. Only write one problem statement per problem checklist.

User goal
Only write one goal per problem checklist. Write the outcome that the audience is trying to achieve when experiencing the problem. THIS IS NOT THE SOLUTION! Be careful here. It's very common for people to write out the solution when trying to describe the goal. Seek to describe the end-result, the outcome, not the solution. You will use this section later when you generate your user story statements.  
User needs You may write one or many user needs per problem checklist. Describe the human expectation that they want to be in place in order to solve the problem. THIS IS NOT THE SOLUTION! THIS IS NOT THE GOAL! Be careful here. It's very common for people to write a solution (i.e. "They need a button..." or "they need to know where their cat is...") when trying to describe the user need. Refer back to the earlier sections in this week's lesson for reminders about needs vs. solutions. This is where the "rubber meets the road," and your knowledge about needs vs. solutions is put to the test.

Consequences to avoid
Make a list of all of the bad things that the user is trying to avoid (successfully or not) when experiencing the problem, and add them here. This provides helpful context for teams when trying to ABC (always be closing) and convincing teams (through their requirements) that the problem is worth solving. You will use this section later when you generate your user story statements.

Workshop Summary:
UX is a scientific field! We UX’ers follow the Scientific Method in our work. We pose hypotheses and build tests to test the hypothesis. They are either true or false. Sometimes, the results are undetermined.

In the context of Agile UX, UX’ers finish one single round of research in a short period of time known as “an iteration”. This could be one week, or two weeks, based on the Agile Method you are following.

This training framework provides a way to follow a repeated cycle of mapping questions and hypotheses to assumptions and points of measurement for the purposes of building a research test.
Workshop Goals:
Pick your top research topics
Identify your assumptions about research topics
Prioritize your assumptions about the topics
Create details about your assumption:
Implications

This research test framework is valuable because it allows teams to always work on the most important assumptions to validate in research at any given time.

Where to keep it:

Workshop Pitch Statement: A workshop that turns research topics into a rigorous, repeatable test plan, treating UX as a science: prioritize topics, form assumptions, map them to questions and measurements, choose methods, and document the test.
What You Need Before You Start: Bring the team (UX Research and UX Strategy lead, but collaborate with all functions) and the topics or problems you want to learn about. Set up the FigJam board with the topic list, assumption table, method-selection guide, and test-plan template. This runs each research iteration of a week or two.
The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What do we want to learn (research topics)?
2. Which are most important to do now?
3. What assumptions do we hold, and what problem, implications, and measurements attach to each?
4. Which research method fits each question?
5. What is our full test plan?
What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with prioritized research topics, an assumption table mapping each to a problem, implications, and ways to test it, chosen methods, and a complete test plan (background, goals, questions, assumptions, methodology, limitations). Done well, it is rigorous enough to repeat and aims at the highest-value assumptions.
Time Needed: One research iteration (about one to two weeks of planning and testing)
Common Pitfalls & Tips: Treat UX as a science: everything starts as a hypothesis you test to true, false, or undetermined. You cannot test everything in one iteration, so prioritize the riskiest, least-certain assumptions. Choose the method from the type of question (generative vs evaluative, what vs why, short vs long). And name the research's limitations honestly.
Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam; it feeds the Research Analysis workshop after testing.

Workshop Brief: This workshop produces the UX Research Plan (and supports analytics and accessibility analyses). A research plan documents a study's goals, questions, methods, and participants; Tech Fleet frames UX as a science, mapping assumptions to hypotheses and measurements so tests can be prioritized and repeated.

Workshop Summary: How does a team know what they will decide after doing all of the research or gathering all of the information? THEY DON’T! They all may have ideas, but they could be totally wrong. It’s best to quickly get to a shippable idea that gets tested than to keep talking about the possibilities of the direction a team could make. Rapid Ideation is just that: Quick (so many ideas get generated from this!) and generative (creative ideas get generated from thin air!), getting teams to the other side of delivery after thinking about all of the possibilities that could occur.
Workshop Goals:
Problem-solve in creative ways

Rapidly generate a lot of ideas to work with

Move ahead with a testable concept
Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Compile a list of your problem statements
2. Translate your problem statements into How Might We statements
3. Prioritize the How Might We statements
4. Vote on the top HMW statements
5. Perform Rapid Ideation (with Crazy 8’s Method)
6. Present the Rapid Ideation
7. Vote on the top choices
8. Write requirements for the decisions you’ve made that will go to design
9. Design and implement and test the solutions you propose
Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
A Rapid Ideation workshop is valuable because it:

Provides room for creative problem-solving that’s collaborative in nature

Provides ways for more than just one perspective to be heard in decision making and ideation

Provides ways for teams to combine ideas quickly, and form cohesive solutions that can be complex
How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Teams can perform this as often as they want for continuous rounds of delivery work that turns into designs and concepts to test and ship.
Who Owns the Workshop?: The UX Strategy hat owns this deliverable. The strategy side of UX is purposeful decision making. Rapid Ideation is where the Research meets the Design. Together, with formed knowledge about current state problems, the strategy hats in the room can come together to ideate on how to solve the problems.
Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its How Might We (HMW) Statements and Sketches.
Additional Details:
When to use:
Teams should do this whenever they feel it fits their needs and outcomes! This is not just something that should happen “after research”. If everything is an assumption, then we can ideate on assumptions without research, and use the ideation as the grounding to validate the ideas with research. This is how the Lean UX and Google Design Sprint methods operate!

How to involve other teams:
Do NOT just include the UX designers in this kind of session. Everyone should get involved in rapid ideation, no matter who you are on the team or what roles you want to play! Everyone has an important perspective to share and ideas that UX Designers may have never even thought of.
Workshop Pitch Statement: A fast, everyone-in session that turns a pile of assumed problems into fresh ideas and narrows them to the ideas worth testing.
What You Need Before You Start: Come in with your research findings or assumed problems (ideally as problem statements) and the audiences you serve. Get the whole team in the room, not just designers, and set up the FigJam board with the How Might We table, the risk/certainty priority matrix, and the Crazy 8's grids. A timer is essential. You do not need finished research; you can ideate on assumptions and validate them afterward.
The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What problems do we assume about the current state, for each audience?
2. How might we solve each one, as a How Might We statement?
3. Which HMWs are the riskiest and least certain, so most worth our ideation time?
4. What are all the ways we might solve them?
5. Which ideas are worth turning into requirements and testing?
What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with prioritized How Might We statements and a set of voted, sketched ideas for the top ones, clear enough to write into requirements and test. Done well, everyone sketched, the group converged without endless debate, and the risky, uncertain problems got the most creative attention.
Time Needed: About 90 minutes (two 8-minute Crazy 8's rounds plus discussion and voting)
Common Pitfalls & Tips: Do not make this designers-only; the best ideas often come from outside UX. Do not skip the risk-and-certainty prioritization, or you will waste time ideating on safe, low-risk problems. Honor the Crazy 8's timing (eight ideas in eight minutes) so speed pushes people past their safe first idea. And do not wait for perfect research; ideate on assumptions and validate after, the way Lean UX and Design Sprints do.
Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam or another quickly editable space, so the HMWs, priorities, and ideas stay easy to revisit and turn into requirements.

Workshop Brief: This workshop moves a team from problems to testable ideas, and it produces two things: How Might We statements and quick sketches. A How Might We statement is a design-thinking tool (popularized by IDEO) that reframes a research insight as an open question, like "how might we make sign-up feel effortless?" The wording matters: "how" assumes there is an answer to find, and "might" keeps the door open to many paths, so the question sparks ideas without locking in one. The sketches come from Crazy 8's, a Design Sprint method where each person draws eight rough ideas in eight minutes, one per box. The whole point is quantity over polish; the tight timer pushes people past their safe first idea and surfaces options they would never have reached by talking. Nothing here is meant to be pretty or final. It is raw fuel for deciding what to test.

Workshop Summary: Storyboards are visual representations of significant points in a storyline, incorporating illustrations and images to support your main idea. It is a powerful tool for structuring a story or adding a narrative element to technical linear sequences, including workflows, operational processes, and user pathways, whether for a customer journey or the hero’s journey. In our case, the storyboard will depict a potential member’s experience with skills and practices measurements.
Workshop Goals:
Tell a story of the current state of the experience for people
Envision what the world could look like in the future
Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Add your audience segments you want to focus on
2. Add your use case scenarios for audiences that you want to storyboard for current and future state
3. Choose the use cases you want to storyboard
4. Everyone break out and create both a CURRENT and FUTURE state storyboard for each use case you choose
Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: Storyboards are valuable because they help everyone visualize what life is like today in different situations for audiences, and what life could be like into the future. It’s a great way to brainstorm and strategize before you make decisions of change.
How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Use this whenever the team wants to picture a user's experience, now or in the future. Revisit it as you learn more from research.
Who Owns the Workshop?: Everyone in all functions on cross-functional teams should be using storyboard to strategize before they decide and build alignment with people who have a stake in the results.
Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Storyboard.
Additional Details:
When to use:
This technique helps your team visualize the real-life activities of your users, empathize with them, find important moments along their journey, and uncover gaps and problems you can address.

Specific use case examples for using a storyboard template also include:
Mapping out a business plan to present to a stakeholder.
Visualizing an upcoming marketing campaign. Include important details and resources needed to launch.
Understanding how users interact with a product or service, especially by mapping out key scenes or touch points within the customer journey.
Workshop Pitch Statement: A workshop where the team draws a user's current and future experience as an eight-panel storyboard, so everyone can see what life is like today and imagine what it could be.
What You Need Before You Start: Bring the team and your audience segments and use case scenarios (from segmentation and discovery). Set up FigJam with the storyboard panels and sticker tools. Everyone participates, and drawing skill is not required.
The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. Which audiences and use cases do we want to storyboard?
2. What does the user's experience look like today, step by step?
3. How do they struggle and feel?
4. What could the experience look like in the future once their problems are solved?
What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with current and future storyboards for each chosen use case, drawn as simple eight-panel stories. Done well, the current one honestly shows today's struggles, and the future one is a creative, specific vision of what could be.
Time Needed: About 10 minutes per storyboard, plus discussion
Common Pitfalls & Tips: Keep it low-fidelity; doodles and emojis are fine as long as the story reads. Always do both current and future. For the future, go wild; it is your blue-sky wish list, so be specific about how each problem gets solved.
Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam with your discovery work.

# How to
  How do you make a storyboard

As a group, draw out a specific user scenario or story in sequential panels (like a comic book). This is commonly done in eight panels and participants are usually given ten minutes to complete the story. 

Make sure to include two versions:

Current Experience 
How does the user experience the product/service in the moment? What do they struggle with? How does it impact their life? How do they feel? What do they wish they had?

Future Experience 
How does the user experience the product/service now that all their problems have gone away? In the future state storyboards, you should be specifically ideating what could be possible to solve the current state problems.  Be specific. Instead of saying "People are confused", say what exactly should be happening, in order to solve the problem of confusion. 

What to include:

The imagery can be very low fidelity (and even use things like emojis, doodling, or pictures) so long as the narrative is communicated.

What to include:

Once the storyboard is complete, come together and analyze it with the whole team, and then you can fill in smaller details that connect the main story points.
  Tip: Future Experience is your wish list, your "blue sky" ideation time. The future storyboards should be creative and depicting what would be and could be! 

This is where you can GO WILD. Remember some of the greatest ideas came through seemingly impossible solutions!

Workshop Name: Audience Segmentation, Goals, Motivations, and Use Cases Workshop Template
Workshop Summary: To properly understand how you should be solving problems for your audiences, teams need to work to understand the day in the life of users. This happens in a variety of ways. It involves a lot of brainstorming, assumption mapping, and research to understand how to communicate goals and motivations of your audiences. Understanding how you want to describe your audience is up to you and the team and the clients involved. You can use Segmentation to describe your audiences from different perspectives: where they live, how they behave, their background, or their socioeconomic status. From there, you can work together to identify the motivations and goals that audiences have, and what kinds of segments are the most valuable to focus on for the business. This workshop helps teams brainstorm about the segmented traits of potential audiences, and communicate what they care about to gain a common understanding.
Workshop Goals:
Build semantic labels around audience segments.
Agree to the audience segment descriptions your team wants to align on.
Brainstorm motivations, goals, and scenarios to support that will be important to audience segments.
Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Identify potential traits of segments based on:
2. Geography
3. Behavior
4. Demographics
5. Socioeconomic status
6. Pick the most impactful traits and describe your audiences you want to focus on.
7. Identify the motivations of the audience segment.
8. Identify the situational goals and life goals that audience segment has in the end-to-end experience.
9. Identify the use case scenarios that are the most impactful to support for each audience segment.
Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
The team can align with clients, stakeholders, and each other about the areas of focus that will bring the most value to audiences based on how they describe the audiences.
The team can base the user research, market research, and implementation of designs based on what they define for segmentation.
How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Do this during discovery, then update it as research teaches you more about your audiences.
Who Owns the Workshop?: The Product Manager hat owns the audience segmentation that should be focused on. As teams do more research over time, the segmentation of audiences changes and evolves. The product manager hat maintains the definitions of target audience segments over time.
Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Buyer Personas and Customer Segmentation.
Additional Details: When to use: during discovery, after sprints begin, when the team is deciding who to build for.
Workshop Pitch Statement: A workshop where the team labels and describes its target audiences by segment, then digs into each one's motivations, goals, and the use cases worth supporting.
What You Need Before You Start: Bring the team and whatever you know about your audiences. Set up the FigJam board with the segmentation fields (geographic, behavioral, demographic, socioeconomic) and the per-audience motivation, goals, and use-case sections. Best early in discovery; owned by the Product Manager hat.
The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What segment traits (geographic, behavioral, demographic, socioeconomic) describe our audiences?
2. Which traits matter most, and how do we label our focus audiences?
3. What motivates each audience, and what are their situational and life goals?
4. Which use case scenarios are most impactful to support?
What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with labeled audience segments, each with its motivations, situational and life goals, and a prioritized set of use cases to support. Done well, the team, clients, and stakeholders share one language for who you serve and why.
Time Needed: A focused session, then refined through research
Common Pitfalls & Tips: Segments are often guesses at first; document them and refine with research. Pick the most impactful traits rather than trying to capture everything. And prioritize the use cases so you focus on what brings the most value.
Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam; the Product Manager maintains it as segments evolve.

  How do you know which work to do first?
In short: you don't, and no one does. It's all just a guess and a judgment call based on what you know. You could get the guess wrong, and Agile is built for quick adjustments when you get it wrong. One needs to embrace this lifestyle in requirements work for Agile teams. You will constantly be guessing which is the correct way to go. "Continuous improvement" all the way. You can use tools like prioritization matrices to rank problems to solve and decide which ones to solve first. The rest is up to what the team decides to put into their release-level vision, and what they learn after they deliver iterations towards the release.

Workshop Brief: This workshop produces Customer Segmentation and Buyer Personas. Segmentation groups an audience by shared traits (demographic, geographic, behavioral, socioeconomic); here the team labels its focus audiences and digs into each one's motivations, goals, and use cases to support.

Workshop Summary: All great case studies have great stories to tell. People in the fields of product management, project management, UX, or other related fields always need to describe the story of humans that are affected by changes that get made. This workshop helps teams concretely tie project deliverables to case study components based on empowered teamwork and self-organized thinking principles.
Workshop Goals:
Identify the key components of a good case study
Ideate about how to get other people on teams involved in case study creation
Map deliverables to case study outcomes
Make informed decisions about how to approach story arcs in case studies
Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Answer questions about your own lived experience and perspective of case studies
2. Map project deliverables to case study outcomes
3. Learn about story arcs
4. Learn about the attributes of a great case study
5. See the parts of case studies broken down from the perspective of a story arc about human beings (instead of the work itself)
Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: This is valuable because it helps individuals who are a part of teamwork see how other kinds of work affects their own success story and case study. It sets expectations for teams about how to be cross-functional in order to share your success at the end in concrete ways.
How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Use this at any point in a project, and again near the end when people are ready to write up their work. It helps to start collecting the story early.
Who Owns the Workshop?: The whole team owns this outcome together! You all work together across different kinds of work to share the outcomes of a case study.
Additional Details: When to use: any time, and especially near the end of a phase when people build their portfolios.
Workshop Pitch Statement: A reflection workshop that prepares each teammate to build a strong case study, the story of their growth and work on the project, by planning for it from the start rather than scrambling at the end.
What You Need Before You Start: Bring the team and your understanding of the project's deliverables and milestones. Set up FigJam with the reflection prompts and the story-driven outline. Best done early, so the team sets the project up to produce good case studies.
The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What makes a good case study, and what makes a bad one?
2. What must the team do, and what events must happen, to produce a great one?
3. How will we work with other teams to produce it?
4. What is the story-driven outline of our case study?
What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with a shared understanding of what a strong case study is and a story-driven outline, plus a plan for the events and collaboration that produce one. Done well, the team sets itself up to tell the story of its growth, not just list deliverables.
Time Needed: A focused reflection session
Common Pitfalls & Tips: A great case study tells the story of your growth and process, not just the artifacts you made. Plan for it during the project (capture events, collaboration, and decisions), not after. And it takes cross-team collaboration to produce, so set that up early.
Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam and carry the outline through the project.

# How to Create a Great Case Study from Any Work!
  How to Create a Great Case Study from Any Work!
  Case studies are crucial for telling your story about how your team collaborated together. Case studies are so challenging because it’s hard to know what information to share, and how to condense it in a compelling manner. You have to tell the story in such a way that keeps the audiences’ attention. This is where you can put on your User Experience hat! They should showcase meaningful problem-solving and concrete outcomes. Really great case studies don’t have a “perfect ending”, just like really great stories may not have a “perfect ending”.  The work will never stop,  you are possibly presenting a small piece of work on a short timeline that will continue after. It probably started before you joined the team too. You still need to showcase impact and progress in your team’s work.
  You Can Tell the Story from Your Timeline
  Although there was work before you started, and there will be work after you stopped, you can still tell a meaningful story. You’ve contributed to a better holistic outcome of progress. You’ve contributed toward solving problems with teams. Your perspective was valuable and should be showcased. You can speak about how you would measure impact or value once the problem is solved even if that’s years from now.
  The previous team’s work
  Your work
  The next team’s work
  Good Case Studies Have...
  A Story Arc
  Everyone loves a great story. There are different ways to tell it, but it should start with some kind of problem and show how it progressed. Try to avoid describing “multiple events” like if you were describing how it all happened. Take the readers there. Envelop them into the story itself, relive the story through the case study with them. There are way to structure a story called “Arcs”, and this template focuses on the arc that depicts three parts: problem, journey, progress.
  Measurable Concrete Outcomes
  You may have heard the phrase “Do the work with the end in mind”. While visuals can be key to showing how the work happened, it’s not enough to add a lot of pictures of your interface designs or produced results. Showing how you measured success, or how you would measure success, is the most important part of showing the work. You can do this in a lot of ways. If you were not in the position to actually measure change, you should show how you would measure change so that readers can see your thought process. Doing this will highlight the potential impact of your decisions as a team.
  A Focus on The “Why”
  Focusing on the reasoning and “why” behind your design decisions in a UX case study is crucial because it reveals your problem-solving mindset and critical thinking skills. Employers and stakeholders aren't just interested in what you designed. They want to understand the logic, research, and trade-offs that guided each choice. By articulating the “why,” you demonstrate that your design isn’t arbitrary or based on trends, but grounded in user needs, business goals, and usability principles. This level of insight differentiates you from others who simply showcase visuals, highlighting your ability to think strategically and collaborate effectively within cross-functional teams.
  User Audience Perspective
  This will ground your work in real human needs and context. UX is not a creative field. UX is an applied science field. We follow the scientific method to test hypotheses. Our product decisions are hypotheses, and we need to show how we tested them. We need to show the data that helped us form the hypotheses. All adjacent roles should follow this structure too. Product owners, business analysts, product designers, UX designers, UX researchers: you also need to showcase user perspective about the problems you are solving. Whatever title you are after, your case study should tell the story about the current state, and how you strategized to make the current state different.
  Conflict to Resolve
  The conflict you resolve could be the user pain points, conflict within the team, or both. Your audiences don’t want to see that you did this work alone. They want to see how your team pulled together to tackle the conflict. They want to see how you progressed through adversity and changing winds. This is an understated strength of teamwork when people face conflict and resolve it to grow together. Discuss in your case study how you grew through the conflict, and how your team and outcomes grew through the conflict.
  Cross-Functional Collaboration
  UX and product work often happens in a team, and sometimes teams isolate themselves based on a department. Employers value designers who can collaborate effectively and contribute to a shared vision, not just produce individual work in a vacuum. Employers who run agile teams want to see your cross-functional collaboration skills meaning how you worked together as a unified team across all kinds of work functions to accomplish an outcome. This is easier said than done. It relies on you to understand the overarching project plan and the work that others did. It relies on you as a teammate getting involved in other work functions so you can tell the story of the context. Showcasing how you worked within a team highlights your communication skills, adaptability, and ability to integrate diverse perspectives into your design process

Workshop Brief: This workshop does not produce a project deliverable; it prepares each teammate's case study, the story of the growth and work they did on the project. It grounds a strong portfolio piece in the real outcomes, collaboration, and process of the work.

Workshop Summary:
This is a continuation of the UX Research Test Plan Workshop.

UX is a scientific field! We UX’ers follow the Scientific Method in our work. We pose hypotheses and build tests to test the hypothesis. They are either true or false. Sometimes, the results are undetermined.

In the context of Agile UX, UX’ers finish one single round of research in a short period of time known as “an iteration”. This could be one week, or two weeks, based on the Agile Method you are following.

This training framework provides a way to follow a repeated cycle of mapping questions and hypotheses to assumptions and points of measurement for the purposes of building a research test. In this workshop, results from research are analyzed based on assumptions.
Workshop Goals:
Analyze research results based on theme.
Form conclusions from research data.
Determine whether assumptions were true, false, or undetermined.
Identify the next priorities for research based on latest test results.
Present summarized results to other kinds of stakeholders.
Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Run the research through the UX Research Test Plan Workshop.
2. Create an affinity map of the results
3. Create the conclusions table
4. Form summarized results to present to stakeholders
Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
This research analysis framework is valuable because it allows teams to analyze their assumptions and present key takeaways.
This helps teams always map their research to an assumption or a research question for better organization.
How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Do this after each round of research, usually once a sprint, so findings turn into decisions while they are fresh.
Who Owns the Workshop?: The UX Research function and UX Strategy function owns this deliverable. Whomever is working in this function should collaborate with other functions to collect necessary input about assumptions or priorities before deciding how to proceed with the research analysis.
Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its UX Audit Report, Research Report, Rainbow Table, Affinity Map, and Research Analysis.
Additional Details:
Where to keep it:
Keep it in Figjam, or some other place where you can keep it over time

How to involve other teams:
Researchers should collaborate with all other team functions including product people, UX designers, and even developers in their research analysis. This provides space for all cross-functional teammates to get involved directly in the results of research before it’s presented to them, and provides ways for other perspectives to be heard.
Workshop Pitch Statement: The after-the-test workshop where a team turns raw research results into clear themes, conclusions about each assumption, and the next research questions, run every sprint.
What You Need Before You Start: Bring the UX Research and UX Strategy leads (with the whole team's input) and your completed test results from the Research Plan workshop. Set up FigJam with the results tables, an affinity-map space, and the assumption-conclusion table. Do this every sprint after testing.
The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What were the raw results of each question, task, and observation?
2. What themes emerge across them?
3. For each assumption, was it true, false, or undetermined?
4. What new research questions has this raised?
5. What do we research next?
What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with documented results, an affinity map of themes, a conclusion for every assumption, and a prioritized set of new research questions. Done well, the analysis clearly says what you learned and what to explore next, and the cycle continues.
Time Needed: A focused session each sprint after testing
Common Pitfalls & Tips: Separate what people said from what they did; observations often matter more than statements. Conclude honestly, including 'undetermined.' And always form new assumptions and questions, since research never stops in agile.
Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam; it feeds the next Research Plan iteration.

Workshop Name: Market Research and Competitive Analysis Workshop Template
Workshop Summary: Competitive analysis is when you look closely at other businesses or products that are similar to yours to see what they do well, what they don’t, and what makes them popular (or not). Product managers do this to make smarter decisions about what features to build, what problems to solve, and how to make their product stand out. Without it, you could end up building something that already exists or doesn’t offer anything better, which means people won’t choose your product.
Workshop Goals:
Understand the market.
Understand your direct and indirect competitors.
Understand features that may set you apart from competitors.
Understand how you can be inspired by other design patterns and conventions that other competitors use.
Define how to uniquely position your product or service in the market you’re launching into.
Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Answer the basic questions
2. Choose the scope of your competitive analysis:
3. Market research
4. Direct and indirect competitor analysis
5. Feature analysis
6. Design pattern analysis
7. Product positioning
8. Perform Market research
9. Perform Direct and indirect competitor analysis
10. Perform Feature analysis
11. Perform Design pattern analysis
12. Perform Product positioning
Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
A competitive analysis is valuable because:

It helps product and service teams differentiate their offerings
It helps justify the direction and strategy for product definitions
It helps your team understand what they should avoid in order to position the best success for the market.
How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Your competitive analysis should not just be drafted once. It needs to be adjusted on a continuous basis based on the changing priorities and decisions on the team. The product strategy team should determine how often they should perform a competitive analysis based on their unique team needs.
Who Owns the Workshop?:
The Product Manager function owns this deliverable. They must:

Perform the research with the full team.
Analyze the results.
Make strategic decisions in their release-level vision and scope based on the analysis.
Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Competitive Analysis, Market Research Analysis, Positioning Statement, Unique Value Proposition, and Product-Market Fit Analysis.
Additional Details:
When to use:
Teams should perform the competitive analysis during discovery, either in initial discovery or continuous discovery.

Where to keep it:
This should be kept and maintained in Figjam or some other place where it can be quickly edited.

How to involve other teams:
The product strategy team must constantly “own” this deliverable and ensure it’s accurate. They need to talk to the other team roles to ensure that they are bought in with the priorities for each role. This is a conversation and collaboration that takes place weekly. The product strategy team may need to keep this artifact up to date daily. This artifact is used for the basis of sprint planning.
Workshop Pitch Statement: A discovery workshop where the team studies its market and competitors, then turns what it learns into a sharp story: where the opportunity is, what sets the product apart, and how to position it.
What You Need Before You Start: Come in with a rough idea of what you are building and who it might serve, plus access to online research and AI tools to speed it up. Have the product strategy team present, and set up the FigJam board with the market-size table, competitor tables, feature chart, and positioning template. You will cite sources as you go, so be ready to look things up.
The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What market segments exist, how big are they, and where is the gap?
2. Who are our direct and indirect competitors, and what do they do well and poorly?
3. How do our features compare, and what is missing in the market?
4. What design patterns should we borrow so the product feels familiar?
5. What makes us different, and how do we position it?
What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with sized market segments and a named opportunity, a filled competitor and feature analysis, a summary of the gaps competitors leave open, and a product positioning statement. Done well, every claim is backed by cited research, and the team can defend why the product is different and worth building.
Time Needed: A large, multi-part analysis run across discovery, not a single sitting; expect several focused sessions
Common Pitfalls & Tips: This is not a one-time draft; the product strategy team keeps it current as priorities shift, and it feeds sprint planning. Scope it to the decision at hand rather than always running all five analyses. And cite your sources for every data point so the analysis stays trustworthy rather than a pile of guesses.
Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam or another quickly editable space, and update it continuously as priorities and findings change.

# ABOUT MARKET RESEARCH
  ABOUT MARKET RESEARCH
  Market research is when you collect information about people who might use your product like what they want, what they buy, and what problems they have. This helps teams build something they actually care about. 

Product managers do market research early in discovery so they don’t waste time or money making something no one wants. It helps them understand the market, define a clear vision, and make smarter decisions from day one.

Market research includes:
Market segments: These are the different groups of people in the market, like teenagers who game, college students who love coffee, or parents who need help with homework apps. Segmenting helps you figure out exactly who you’re building for.
Market size: This tells you how many people are in each segment and how much money they might spend. A big market size means more potential customers and more money to be made.
Market opportunity: This is where you spot a gap, something people want but aren’t getting. If your research shows that gamers want a social app with fewer ads and there’s nothing like that, that’s a clear opportunity.

How it affects the product vision:
Market research shapes the product’s purpose and direction. For example, if you find that students want a fast, ad-free study app, the product vision might be: “The most focused and ad-free homework helper for high school students.” Every decision going forward is based on that vision.

How to perform market research:
Identify the possible market segments in the same space as your product or service.
Identify the size of each market segment in market cap.
Identify the opportunities that exist in the markets so that you can build the best opportunity for the market and your business.

# ABOUT COMPETITOR ANALYSIS
  ABOUT COMPETITOR ANALYSIS
  Direct and indirect competitor analysis is when you study businesses or products that are either exactly like yours (direct competitors) or similar but not the same (indirect competitors). This analysis helps define what makes your product unique and how it can stand out.

For product managers, doing this analysis early in the discovery phase is important because it helps them understand the competition, know what features customers are used to, and identify any gaps in the market. This analysis affects the product vision by showing where there’s room to stand out. 

To do a direct and indirect competitor analysis:
Identify the questions you want to answer about competitors unique to your project
Identify the direct competitors in the market segment
Analyze their strengths and weaknesses: What do they do well? What are they missing?
Identify opportunities: Look for features or needs that are unmet, and think about how your product can fill that gap.

# ABOUT DESIGN PATTERN ANALYSIS
  ABOUT DESIGN PATTERN ANALYSIS
  Design pattern analysis is when product designers study how other apps or websites are built—like how buttons look, how menus open, or how people sign up—to see what works well and what users are already used to. It’s kind of like looking at how popular games design their controls so yours feels familiar and easy to use.

Doing this early in discovery is important because it helps designers make smarter choices before they start building. It saves time, avoids confusing users, and keeps the product feeling modern and simple. It also helps shape the product vision—if the vision is to be “the easiest budgeting app for teens,” then the design patterns should support simplicity, clarity, and fun. This helps create a product that looks good, works well, and feels just right for the people using it.

How to do a design pattern analysis:
Choose similar products: Look at apps or websites that solve the same problem.
Study their design patterns: Notice how they handle navigation, buttons, forms, layouts, and colors.
Compare the patterns: What’s common across all of them? What feels easy or hard?
Decide what to use or improve: Keep the helpful patterns and change or improve anything that seems confusing or outdated.

# ABOUT FEATURE ANALYSIS
  ABOUT FEATURE ANALYSIS
  Feature comparison analysis is when you look at your product and compare its features to other similar products on the market. 

Product managers do this early in discovery to understand what competitors offer, what customers like or don’t like, and what’s missing. It helps them avoid building something that’s already out there and instead focus on features that are better, different, or more valuable.

This analysis shapes the product vision by showing where the biggest opportunities are—like if all music apps have ads, maybe the vision becomes “the best free, ad-free music experience.” It helps define what makes the product special and worth building.

To do a feature comparison analysis:
Pick your direct and indirect competitors (see competitor analysis)
List their features. What does each one offer?
Compare them side by side. Use a table or chart to see what's common, what's unique, and what's missing.
Describe the feature-related gaps or opportunities. Look for features people want but no one offers well.

# ABOUT PRODUCT POSITIONING
  ABOUT PRODUCT POSITIONING
  Product positioning is a way to describe how you will approach describing your product. This includes how you make people see and understand what your product is, who it’s for, and why it’s better or different from others. Think of it like giving your product a “personality” and a spot in the customer’s mind—like “the fastest sports drink for teen athletes” or “the easiest music app for beginners.”

Product managers figure this out early during discovery so they can build a product that connects with the right audience. If you don’t know how to position your product, people might not understand why it matters, or it might seem just like everything else. It affects the product vision by helping define what the product will be known for and why it exists. 

To perform product positioning analysis:
Identify your target audience: Who is the product for?
Understand what your target audiences care about: What problems do they have? What do they value?
Compare with competitors: What are other products known for?
Find your unique spot: What makes your product different or better from competitors?
Write a product positioning statement.

This analysis shapes the product vision by showing where the biggest opportunities are—like if all music apps have ads, maybe the vision becomes “the best free, ad-free music experience.” It helps define what makes the product special and worth building.

To do a feature comparison analysis:
Pick your direct and indirect competitors (see competitor analysis)
List their features. What does each one offer?
Compare them side by side. Use a table or chart to see what's common, what's unique, and what's missing.
Describe the feature-related gaps or opportunities. Look for features people want but no one offers well.

# ABOUT DESIGN PATTERN ANALYSIS
  ABOUT DESIGN PATTERN ANALYSIS
  Design pattern analysis is when product designers study how other apps or websites are built—like how buttons look, how menus open, or how people sign up—to see what works well and what users are already used to. It’s kind of like looking at how popular games design their controls so yours feels familiar and easy to use.

Doing this early in discovery is important because it helps designers make smarter choices before they start building. It saves time, avoids confusing users, and keeps the product feeling modern and simple. It also helps shape the product vision—if the vision is to be “the easiest budgeting app for teens,” then the design patterns should support simplicity, clarity, and fun. This helps create a product that looks good, works well, and feels just right for the people using it.

How to do a design pattern analysis:
Choose similar products: Look at apps or websites that solve the same problem.
Study their design patterns: Notice how they handle navigation, buttons, forms, layouts, and colors.
Compare the patterns: What’s common across all of them? What feels easy or hard?
Decide what to use or improve: Keep the helpful patterns and change or improve anything that seems confusing or outdated.

# ABOUT PRODUCT POSITIONING
  ABOUT PRODUCT POSITIONING
  Product positioning is a way to describe how you will approach describing your product. This includes how you make people see and understand what your product is, who it’s for, and why it’s better or different from others. Think of it like giving your product a “personality” and a spot in the customer’s mind—like “the fastest sports drink for teen athletes” or “the easiest music app for beginners.”

Product managers figure this out early during discovery so they can build a product that connects with the right audience. If you don’t know how to position your product, people might not understand why it matters, or it might seem just like everything else. It affects the product vision by helping define what the product will be known for and why it exists. 

To perform product positioning analysis:
Identify your target audience: Who is the product for?
Understand what your target audiences care about: What problems do they have? What do they value?
Compare with competitors: What are other products known for?
Find your unique spot: What makes your product different or better from competitors?
Write a product positioning statement.

Workshop Brief: This workshop grounds a team in its market and turns that understanding into a sharp story, producing five connected outputs. A competitive analysis studies a handful of direct competitors (and a couple of indirect ones) across usability, features, and value to find gaps worth filling. A market research analysis pulls together data on market size, customers, and trends so big bets rest on evidence, not hunches. From that, the team writes a positioning statement, an internal compass of how the product is different and for whom (For [target], [product] is the [difference] among [category] because [reason]), and a unique value proposition, the sharper, customer-facing sentence of the single main benefit. Finally, product-market fit gets judged; it is less a single number and more a set of signals, like whether people are using the product as fast as you can ship it and whether word of mouth is spreading (a common check is Sean Ellis's rule that 40 percent of users would be "very disappointed" to lose it). Together these move a team from "we think there's a market" to a clear, defensible story about who the product is for and why it wins.

Workshop Summary: A customer experience map is an essential piece of documenting the current and future customer experience for different audiences. It’s a great communication tool for teams to help others build empathy and understand how things work today for user audiences. This workshop helps teams create customer experience maps. It explains the difference between user journey maps and Customer Experience Maps, which are similar but different deliverables for different purposes. Both work together to help teams communicate the current experience and the future experience.
Workshop Goals:
Map each step in the experience for each audience
Identify pain points in each step of the experience for each audience
Strategize around how to change the current experience based on pain points and business goals.
Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Map the current customer experience in a flow chart for each audience
2. Identify pain points, ideas, and questions in the flow charts
3. Map the future customer experience in a flow chart for each audience
4. Outline how the experience will work through the customer lifecycle funnel: awareness, engagement, consideration, conversion, retention, and loyalty.
Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
A customer experience map is valuable because it:

Aligns teams in understanding the current steps in the experience for each audience today
Helps teams see where pain points are introduced in the experience
Helps teams build empathy with users about the current experience and user audiences
How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Your team doesn’t just produce a customer experience map once. As they proceed through continuous discovery, they should come back to the customer experience maps and update them as they learn new things about the experience today and plan the experience for the future.
Who Owns the Workshop?:
The UX functions on the team own the customer experience maps (UX research, UX design, UX strategy, UX writing). They must:

Draft the first customer experience map iteration
Collect other teams’ thoughts on what needs to be included
Collect stakeholder thoughts on what needs to be included
Collect user thoughts on what needs to be included
Iterate on the customer experience maps as they learn from continuous discovery
Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its Customer Experience Diagram.
Additional Details:
When to use:
Teams should produce the initial customer experience map during discovery, and they should never stop updating the customer experience maps after each round of research. They should utilize continuous discovery to keep learning about the customer experience map and keep documenting it over time.

Where to keep it:
The customer experience maps should be kept and maintained in Figjam or some other place where it can be quickly edited.

How to involve other teams:
All teammates across all functions should collaborate together to produce the customer experience maps. All perspectives should be heard and collaborate together.
Workshop Pitch Statement: A cross-functional workshop that maps each audience's current and future experience as a flow chart through the customer lifecycle funnel, surfacing pain points and the strategies to fix them.
What You Need Before You Start: Bring the whole team and your discovery work: personas, empathy maps, and research. Set up the FigJam board with the funnel stages (awareness, engagement, consideration, conversion, retention, loyalty) and the color legend. This works best after personas and empathy maps.
The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What are the steps in each audience's current experience, funnel stage by funnel stage?
2. Where are the pain points, ideas, and open questions?
3. What should the future experience look like?
4. What strategies would solve the current pain points?
What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with current and future experience flow charts for each audience, pain points and strategies marked, mapped across the whole customer lifecycle funnel. Done well, the team shares a clear picture of how things work today and a plan for how they should work.
Time Needed: A substantial session, then updated through discovery
Common Pitfalls & Tips: Do not confuse this with a user journey map. A CX map is a flow chart across the whole funnel for all audiences; a journey map is a table for a single audience. Use the color legend (red = pain, yellow = idea, blue = question, green = strategy). And never call it done; update it through continuous discovery.
Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam and update it after each round of research.

  Current User Journeys
  We will document the current customer experience for each audience to define the current sentiments and opportunities. In the table below, write as many details as you know about the current experience. Complete the table to outline all of the steps, actions, and details involved in the current experience today.   # Section 3
    Awareness
The awareness stage is the most vital stage, as it’s the start of the customer journey. In the awareness stage, prospects and leads will be made aware of your brand. 
The idea here is simple. The customer has an issue, want, or need, and your brand is presented as a solution — nothing more, nothing less. You want to get them thinking about your brand, product, or service. This is usually done through some strategically placed ads or organic campaigns that bring top-of-the-funnel traffic.
    Credit: https://encharge.io/customer-lifecycle-marketing/
    Engagement
Let’s assume you run a real estate agency. Whenever someone makes a big purchase, they tend to reach out and voluntarily engage with the brand before following through with a conversion. Maybe the lead will follow you on social media, schedule a consultation, or even send an email asking some questions. 

You can see how making this effort beforehand is necessary for a larger purchase. However, it’s not always considered a part of the customer lifecycle with everyday purchases like an in-store product or a subscription to a company like Netflix. 

Put in other words, if you run a B2B business, you most likely will need to include this stage as a part of your customer lifecycle, but that might not be the case if you are in the B2C space.
    Consideration
Now it’s time to really show the lead what you’re made of. The consideration stage is where they will take everything they’ve learned and evaluate which brand best suits their needs. The goal here is to nurture your leads and constantly but subtly remind them that you’re the best option. Typically, this is considered the middle of the funnel.

There are a few ways to go about this, but leads in this stage must be handled with care. One wrong move on your part, missed opening, or even poorly worded message can send the lead marching in the opposite direction.
To avoid that, here are some questions that your messaging should be answering for leads in this stage:
What is unique about your product?
What specific features set you apart from the rest?
What can you add to sweeten the deal and outshine your competition?

Here, it’s all about pushing the lead to pull the trigger. For a lot of brands, that means bringing out the big guns and doing whatever it takes. But, at this point in the funnel, your advertising strategy can either make or break you. This goes back to what we were saying before and understanding your customers through-and-through. Knowing precisely what leads need to see at this stage can end up saving you some big bucks in ad spend.
    Conversion
Congratulations! You’ve just made another sale and gained a new customer. Your job is done. Or is it? 
In truth, the battle is only half-won at this point. Sure, you made a sale, and (hopefully!) your profit margins have gone up, but it’s not exactly over.
You still have to prove that what you’ve provided for the customer is valuable for them. After all, your customers are not just another dollar sign in the company’s bank account. You’ve started a relationship with this customer, and you need to make sure it stays strong.
How’s that done? 
Well, for a lot of companies, the end goal is always conversion. Although that’s not entirely wrong, you still have to think about a few things to knock off the customers’ socks. 
Things like:
How can you make the onboarding process as quick, easy, and enjoyable as possible?
How can you structure this relationship so that the customer can potentially make another purchase?
How can you improve the relationship and the customer’s experience with your product/service by upselling? (Keep in mind, this is not as simple as suggesting a more expensive option).
    Retention
The journey doesn’t end with a conversion. Conversion simply opens up the door to more possibilities. 

This all narrows down to retention, how you treat the customer after the sale, and what you plan on doing to maintain that relationship.

Car salespeople do a great job at this, and it’s worth taking a chapter or two from their book. If you’ve ever bought a car from a car lot, think about your experience there. Sure, there will be some horror stories, but the vast majority of people always mention the high level of service. Using the 3 points above, let’s think about how a good car salesman executes them.

They always show you all odds and ends of the car, showcasing all the cool gadgets and features that you’ll get to enjoy.
The salesman always makes sure you know their name, gives you their card and becomes your best friend on that lot. This ensures that you’ll think of them next time you want to buy a car or suggest where to buy a car to friends or family.
A large majority of a car salesman’s job is making calls to previous customers and telling them about the new offers, trade-in deals, and end-of-the-year sales they have so that they can get more money out of you. If the experience is good the first time, why wouldn’t you want to buy a better car from a great salesman?

That might be a lot of information for a single point, but it’s all to prove that the funnel stages don’t necessarily stop with a conversion.
    Loyalty
We’ve all heard it before. Companies thank their “loyal customers” and offer them the best of what they have to offer. Why?
 
The simple answer is that a loyal customer, one that has stuck with your brand, made several purchases, and gotten to know you as much as you have gotten to know them, is not just a customer anymore. They are brand advocates.

It means that you have someone that bleeds your brand colors, someone who would readily recommend you to friends and family, and someone that brings your company value in more ways than just money.

Customer lifecycle marketing is tricky at this point because you have to put in a ton of effort to get a customer to this stage. Few people will reach this point of the funnel, but that’s nothing to be upset about. They made it here because they’re fans of your brand. That means that their contributions need to be recognized, and they need to be treated like royalty.

Workshop Brief: This workshop produces the Customer Experience Diagram, a flow chart of an audience's end-to-end experience across the lifecycle funnel (awareness through loyalty). It is distinct from a user journey map (a single-audience table); the CX map is broader, showing all audiences and touchpoints.

Workshop Summary: A user journey map is an essential piece of documenting the current experience for different audiences. It’s a great communication tool for teams to help others build empathy and understand how things work today for user audiences. This workshop helps teams create user journey maps. It explains the difference between user journey maps and Customer Experience Maps, which are similar but different deliverables for different purposes. Both work together to help teams communicate the current experience.
Workshop Goals:
Map each step in the experience for each audience
Identify pain points in each step of the experience for each audience
Identify sentiments about each step for each audience
Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Produce one journey map per audience
2. Identify the steps involved in the current experience for each audience
3. Identify the common tasks and common audiences involved per step
4. Identify the sentiment at each step
5. Identify the KPI’s for each step
Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
A journey map is valuable because it:

Aligns teams in understanding the current steps in the experience for each audience today
Helps teams see where pain points are introduced in the experience
Helps teams build empathy with users about the current experience and user audiences
How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Your team doesn’t just produce a user journey map once. As they proceed through continuous discovery, they should come back to the user journey maps and update them as they learn new things about the experience today.
Who Owns the Workshop?:
The UX functions on the team own the user journey maps (UX research, UX design, UX strategy, UX writing). They must:

Draft the first journey map iteration
Collect other teams’ thoughts on what needs to be included
Collect stakeholder thoughts on what needs to be included
Collect user thoughts on what needs to be included
Iterate on the user journey maps as they learn from continuous discovery
Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its User Journey Map.
Additional Details:
When to use:
Teams should produce the initial journey map during discovery, and they should never stop updating the journey map after each round of research. They should utilize continuous discovery to keep learning about the journey and keep documenting it over time.

Where to keep it:
The user journey map should be kept and maintained in Figjam or some other place where it can be quickly edited.

How to involve other teams:
All teammates across all functions should collaborate together to produce the user journey maps. All perspectives should be heard and collaborate together.
Workshop Pitch Statement: A workshop that lays out a single audience's journey as a table, step by step through the customer lifecycle funnel, capturing their tasks, feelings, pain points, and success measures.
What You Need Before You Start: Bring the team and your discovery work: personas, empathy maps, use case scenarios, and research. Set up the FigJam board with the journey table and the funnel stages. This works best during discovery, after personas and empathy maps.
The Core Questions You're Answering:
For a single audience:
1. What steps do they go through, and which funnel stage does each belong to?
2. What tasks and pain points happen at each step?
3. How do they feel at each step?
4. What KPIs would measure success, and what ideas could improve it?
What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with a journey table for the audience: each step tagged to a funnel stage, with description, tasks, pain points, sentiment, KPIs, and improvement ideas. Done well, it reads like a narrative of one real person's experience.
Time Needed: A focused session per audience, then updated through discovery
Common Pitfalls & Tips: A journey map is for a single audience in a table, unlike the CX map's all-audience flow chart. Base the steps on real use case scenarios, and capture honest sentiment (the emoji scale) at each step. Update it as research evolves.
Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam and update it after research.

A large majority of a car salesman’s job is making calls to previous customers and telling them about the new offers, trade-in deals, and end-of-the-year sales they have so that they can get more money out of you. If the experience is good the first time, why wouldn’t you want to buy a better car from a great salesman?

That might be a lot of information for a single point, but it’s all to prove that the funnel stages don’t necessarily stop with a conversion.
    Loyalty
We’ve all heard it before. Companies thank their “loyal customers” and offer them the best of what they have to offer. Why?
 
The simple answer is that a loyal customer, one that has stuck with your brand, made several purchases, and gotten to know you as much as you have gotten to know them, is not just a customer anymore. They are brand advocates.

It means that you have someone that bleeds your brand colors, someone who would readily recommend you to friends and family, and someone that brings your company value in more ways than just money.

Customer lifecycle marketing is tricky at this point because you have to put in a ton of effort to get a customer to this stage. Few people will reach this point of the funnel, but that’s nothing to be upset about. They made it here because they’re fans of your brand. That means that their contributions need to be recognized, and they need to be treated like royalty.

Workshop Summary: How does anyone know which work to decide, or which features to include, or which research to do first? YOU DON’T! You make the best judgment you have at the time and build consensus with the team to decide. Using tools like a prioritization matrix helps you decide quickly based on categories that matter to you. This workshop builds a templated process for a team to prioritize work based on risk and certainty, or effort and value, using what’s called a “MOSCOW” Matrix (which stands for Must, Should, Could, Won’t)
Workshop Goals:
Prioritize your work based on risk and certainty, or effort and value
Choose the top items to work on now vs. later
Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Add your work items in a common space together as a team
2. Choose whether you will prioritize based on:
3. Risk and certainty
4. Effort and value
5. Dot vote on the top work items to choose
6. Finalize your top priorities
Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: A priority matrix is valuable because it helps teams quickly categorize work and choose the things they want to work on first.
How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Use this whenever the team has more to do than it can handle and needs to decide what comes first. Revisit it as priorities change.
Who Owns the Workshop?: Everyone in all functions on cross-functional teams should be using prioritization matrices to decide their work items when they are uncertain about the path ahead.
Expected Outcomes:
A list of “backlogged” work
A list of the top priorities of work
Additional Details: When to use: during discovery, after sprints begin, any time the team needs to pick what to work on next.
Workshop Pitch Statement: A team session that turns a messy pile of possible work into a clear, voted list of what to do next, using a simple priority matrix when the path ahead is uncertain.
What You Need Before You Start: Bring the whole cross-functional team and the work items or problems you're weighing (from discovery, requirements, or team ideas). Decide nothing yet; just gather them. Set up the FigJam board with the two priority matrices and the voting stars ready.
The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What work and future tasks can we identify as a team?
2. Will we prioritize by risk and certainty, or by effort and value?
3. Where does each item fall on the matrix?
4. Which items rise to the top once we vote?
What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with a backlog of identified work and a clear, voted set of top priorities for the next iteration. Done well, the team built the ranking together, so people trust and support the order even knowing it is a judgment call that may change.
Time Needed: About 45 to 60 minutes
Common Pitfalls & Tips: Hold the board's honest point: no one truly knows the right order; it is a judgment call, and agile is built to adjust. Pick one lens (risk/certainty or effort/value), not both at once. Use more than one voting round if the top is not clear.
Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in FigJam or your backlog tool, and re-prioritize as you learn.

Workshop Summary: An audience persona represents traits about your audience. They help you team build for the needs of your audiences instead of building based on guess work. Personas don’t represent one person, but rather an entire audience, and should be generic to fit traits across all people within an audience. You do not need to know everything about your audience to create a persona! You can create a “proto-persona” full of guesses, and use it as a basis for assumption forming and assumption testing in UX work. The persona needs to be updated over time as you learn more about your audience.
Workshop Goals:
Build empathy with the user base
Communicate your audiences’ perspectives
Communicate your audiences’ main goals
Communicate your audiences’ user-centered considerations like demographics and accessibility
Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Identify your target audiences
2. Fill out the information for each audience:
3. Demographics
4. Where they go for information
5. Common tools
6. Accessibility needs
7. User goals
8. Motivations
9. Values
10. Pain points
11. Create a visual result of each audience persona based on the template provided
Why Is This Workshop Valuable?:
Audience personas are valuable because they:

Help teams understand the perspective and mental models of their audiences
Communicate the user-centered nature of user needs by way of appealing to the user perspective and user behavior
How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Teams should revisit the personas whenever they do research so that they can document the changes in their understanding about user behavior and user perspective.
Who Owns the Workshop?: The UX function owns this deliverable. This could be created by the UX research function, UX design function, UX writing function, or UX strategy function.
Expected Outcomes: By the end of this workshop, the team will have produced its User Personas, Proto Personas, and Buyer Personas.
Additional Details:
When to use:
Teams should first create audience personas during discovery, and continue iterating on them as they progress in continuous discovery efforts.

Where to keep it:
Keep this in Figma and Notion for project repository hand off.

How to involve other teams:
Every team function should be involved in this workshop. You need all of the cross-functional perspectives to weigh in on what they think about the user audience you are designing for.
Workshop Pitch Statement: A workshop where the team builds a rich profile of each key audience, capturing who they are, what they need, and what gets in their way, so design decisions rest on real people.
What You Need Before You Start: Bring the whole cross-functional team and whatever you know or have researched about your audiences. Set up the FigJam board with a persona section to copy per audience. If research is thin, start with proto-personas (best guesses) and refine as you learn.
The Core Questions You're Answering:
For each audience:
1. Who are they (demographics)?
2. Where do they go for information?
3. What accessibility and social considerations apply?
4. What tools do they use today?
5. What are their life and situational goals?
6. What motivates them?
7. What are their common tasks?
8. What are their pain points?
What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with a filled persona for each key audience, built from every function's input, with assumptions flagged for research. Done well, the personas feel like real people the team can design for, not vague labels.
Time Needed: About 15 to 20 minutes per audience
Common Pitfalls & Tips: If you lack research, these are proto-personas (educated guesses); label them as such and validate later. Build them cross-functionally, and revisit as research changes your understanding. Where it matters, distinguish user personas (who uses it) from buyer personas (who decides to buy).
Where to Keep the Output: Keep it in Figma and Notion for the project repository hand-off.

Workshop Brief: This workshop builds shared understanding of a user, producing an empathy map and, alongside it, audience personas. An empathy map is a simple visualization of what a user says, thinks, does, and feels; the classic version (Dave Gray, refined by Nielsen Norman Group) uses those four quadrants. One thing to honor here: Tech Fleet's board uses a richer six-prompt, first-person version (I Think, I Act, I Feel, I Say, I Value, I'm Motivated By), so follow the board's six, not the classic four. The goal is the same either way: get everything the team knows or assumes about a user into one place so decisions rest on a shared picture instead of scattered opinions. A persona is a semi-fictional character standing in for a segment of users, and a buyer persona specifically represents the person who decides to purchase, who is not always the person who uses the product. Built from research, or as quick proto-personas when research is thin, these keep the team designing for real people rather than a vague "user."

Workshop Summary: This is a template slide deck built in Figma that cross-functional teams can use to provide results presentations for research as they continue doing discovery in their work.
Workshop Goals:
Share research results in a clear, simple way
Help others understand what the team learned
Show what the team recommends doing next
Workshop Steps to Complete:
1. Copy the slide template
2. Make it your own content
3. Publish to the client
Why Is This Workshop Valuable?: Research only helps if people understand it. A clear presentation turns findings into decisions the whole team and stakeholders can act on.
How Often Should You Do the Workshop?: Use it after each round of research, when the team is ready to share results, usually once a sprint.
Who Owns the Workshop?: The UX Research function owns this workshop and is responsible for running it with the team.
Expected Outcomes:
Introduction
Background
Working assumptions
Research Goals
Research Questions
Top Conclusions
Full Results
Strategy Recommendations
Future Work Recommendations
Additional Details: When to use: after a round of research, when it is time to share results with the team or stakeholders.
Workshop Pitch Statement: A workshop for turning analyzed research into a clear, honest presentation that helps the team and stakeholders understand what users need and decide what to do next.
What You Need Before You Start: Bring your completed research analysis (findings and conclusions) and the presentation slide template. Know your audience for the presentation (team, stakeholders, or client). Set up the slides with room for findings, conclusions, and recommendations.
The Core Questions You're Answering:
1. What are the key findings, and what do they mean?
2. Who does the data represent, and what are its limits?
3. What should the team do about it?
4. What are the next steps?
What \"Done Well\" Looks Like: You leave with a presentation that conveys the key findings, their meaning, the data's limits, and clear, actionable recommendations. Done well, it builds empathy for users and aligns everyone on what to do next.
Time Needed: A focused session to build and present
Common Pitfalls & Tips: Present truthfully and responsibly: say who the data represents and name its limitations. Lead with the findings and what they mean, not a dump of raw data. And translate findings into recommendations stakeholders can act on.
Where to Keep the Output: Keep the slides with your research deliverables.

  Mapping Assumptions to Implications, Problems, and Direct Measurements (Questions / Tasks / Observations) to Test the Assumptions
  When setting up research, one must put on their Scientist hat and perform the Scientific Method. Everything starts with a hypothesis or assumption about problems. Every topic of research breaks down to many assumptions of problems in the current state of the world. You use to set up questions to form an experiment to test the assumptions your team has. Those assumptions can be true, false, or undetermined from your testing. Agile teams test rapidly, and may get research done in one or two weeks at a time with continuous recruitment and “Guerrilla Testing” mechanisms.
